Source: Business Insider Score: 5.78
The US Navy is testing whether it can robotically refuel naval drones at sea, a capability that could allow them to operate for longer in higher-threat waters. Uncrewed surface vessels may not need a crew, but they still need fuel to operate. The recent test is a step toward a fully autonomous refueling process that Navy officials say could eventually let the service send uncrewed vessels into dangerous waters for longer without human support elements. The Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division shared details Wednesday of a recent refueling demonstration involving the remotely controlled T38 USV built by Maritime Tactical Systems Inc. and a towable capture-and-connection robotic refueling system made by Sealartec. During the testing in the waters off Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek-Fort Story in Virginia, the drone and the refueling system completed dozens of capture, refuel, and release exercises. Four hundred gallons of fuel were transferred to the T38. The immediate problem the Navy is trying to solve is tied to the Navy's testing of hypersonic and other long-range weapons. Those tests, "where flight profiles can extend thousands of miles beyond fixed-range boundaries," can "require data-collection assets to be distributed across a vast area," Spencer Holloway, director of the division's Blue Water Instrumentation Future Capabilities Office, said in a release. Naval drones are useful for gathering that data, but having to return for fuel cuts into their time on station. Holloway said that "every time an unmanned vessel must return to port for fuel, we lose persistence, reduce coverage and redundancy, and interrupt the mission." The Navy sees a broader application as well. "This will allow us to have greater reliance on unmanned vessels instead of manned, and we can push the USV into higher threat areas without risking manned vessels and personnel," Ronald Raymer, branch head for capability, innovation, science and technology integration at US Fleet Forces Command, said in the release. "It will also allow us to distribute greater capability into an area without having to invest in large expensive manned vessels," he said. The August demonstration was not fully autonomous. The Navy's next step is a complete end-to-end test in which a drone boat can meet up with a robotic refueling system, approach it, connect, take on fuel, disconnect, and return to its mission without operator control every step of the way. To do that, Holloway said, the systems involved will need more precise maneuvering and better local positioning.

item.title: OpenAI is about to make its biggest push yet into the legal industry
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.75
OpenAI wants to sell large enterprises on its technology. Now, it's taking its case to law firms. The ChatGPT maker is planning to launch new integrations with third-party legal software companies, according to people familiar with the matter. An OpenAI spokesperson declined to comment. The company has been in talks with multiple legal software providers about allowing OpenAI's chatbot to plug into their tools and data sources, the people said. This way, lawyers could update a file, negotiate contracts, or search a legal database, without leaving ChatGPT. Law firms are under pressure from clients to move faster and show they're not billing associates for work that software can do. In-house legal teams are looking for ways to automate more work themselves, so they can send less to outside counsel and shrink their legal bills. That demand has produced a flood of startups addressing legal work. For years, those companies have built on top of large language models supplied by frontier research labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Now the labs appear to want a closer relationship with the users themselves. Anthropic and Google have both begun packaging their models as products for legal departments and law firms, selling directly to enterprises rather than only supplying the models themselves. That effort has been rippling through the public markets. Anthropic's February contract-review plugin helped ignite the "SaaSpocalypse," a stock sell-off driven by fears that AI companies could absorb work once handled by stand-alone software. OpenAI enters the legal market with an unusual advantage. ChatGPT is already the best-known chatbot among the lawyers it hopes to win over. A Law360 survey found ChatGPT was the profession's most-used tool, with 54% of respondents reporting they use it, ahead of Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Harvey, and Claude. But the consumer brand is also a hurdle in a profession where confidentiality and precision are paramount. Lawyers may trust ChatGPT to plan their holidays in St. Barths. Persuading them that it belongs inside a firm's most sensitive workflows is another matter. Chatbots have already landed lawyers in hot water with judges for making up cases and mangling their meanings. The company is making its legal push three months after hiring Jason Boehmig, an executive who spent more than a decade figuring out the slow, messy business of selling software to lawyers. He had left a Big Law job to start Ironclad, a company that helps corporate legal departments manage contracts. Lawyers will be watching OpenAI's launch closely. The tech industry, meanwhile, is about to find out how much room the company intends to leave them.

item.title: What smart people in business and tech are saying about AI bans for schools
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.67
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani introduced a one-year ban on AI in schools, which he said could affect 600,000 public school students. And the tech world has a lot to say. On Wednesday, Mamdani proposed a moratorium that would ban the use of AI in schools for children from 2-K — school for two-year-olds — to eighth grade. High school students will get "twice-yearly AI critical thinking modules." The ban also includes screen time restrictions adjusted for the students' grade level. The same day, Los Angeles Unified School District, the second-largest school district in the US, introduced its own moratorium on AI for the rest of the school year. It would apply to all students, including those in high school, but only on district-owned devices and student accounts. Many in the tech world have taken to social media to criticize Mamdani's AI ban, calling it counterproductive to restrict a technology that could be as transformational as the internet or computers. Mamdani's plan does not require city council approval. Chancellor Kamar Samuels has already issued the moratorium as official NYC Public Schools guidance, stating that student-facing generative AI software "is not permitted" in grades K-8 during the 2026-27 school year. However, some executives have called the moratorium a measured response to a technology with still-unclear ramifications for young, developing minds. Here's what smart people are saying about the AI bans for school students. Sriram Krishnan, a former senior White House policy advisor on AI Sriram Krishnan, a tech executive and former senior White House policy advisor on AI under the second Trump administration, said AI's impact on development is unknown and that it makes sense not to "automate cognitive skills" before kids can acquire them. "Kids need to struggle with all the reading writing math research and reasoning to develop these skills," Krishnan said on X on Thursday, "AI will just remove the friction." "This is the age when foundational skills are formed, adults know this skill so automating with ai can be ok vs a 10 year old who never learns may not," Krishnan added. Zach Tratar, engineering leader at Notion AI and angel Investor Zach Tratar, an engineering lead at Notion AI, wrote on X that AI's effects on children should remain experimental until we learn more. "I'm a pro-AI techno-optimist at heart," Tratar said on Thursday. "But I also remember when we all thought simply connecting people on the internet would make communities healthier," Tratar added. "And when we didn't know if Tiktok would damage our brains." Noah Fichter, CEO of Scout Noah Fichter, the CEO of Scout, an AI startup in the 2025 Y-combinator cohort, wrote on X on Thursday that the tech world's reaction to the AI ban in schools makes him feel "frustrated." "Schools have no literally idea what to do about AI," Fichter said. "Especially when many of the school-specific chatbots we're putting in front of kids are actively decreasing scores!" "Seems pretty obvious to me that Mandani & co spent time in schools, realized the chaos these tools are causing, and decided that we need to take a second to breathe to actually figure it out," Fichter added. Sarah Shirazyan, lecturer at Stanford Law School Sarah Shirazyan, a lecturer in law at Stanford Law School and a research fellow at the Hoover Institution, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Thursday that she expects AI in classrooms to be a big topic for public debate and an issue in elections. "The truth is nobody knows what's the right approach, everyone is experimenting and the moratorium reads to me as let's take time to understand the evidence--aka prove AI works for learning," Shirazyan said. "Having said that, I tell my own Stanford Law students all the time: 'Use your brain first,'" Shirazyan added. Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth and Investment Management Ross Gerber, CEO of financial advisory firm Gerber Kawasaki Wealth and Investment Management, said in a post on X on Thursday that he did the opposite of banning his own children from using AI. "All the kids use AI already. What a goof," Gerber said. "I remember when they told me I couldn't use the computer- go use the typewriter they said." Dylan Itzikowitz, tech investor and partner at South Park Commons Dylan Itzikowit, a tech investor, posted on X on Thursday that AI could have been the "great equalizer" of education. "Wealthy kids won't be affected by this. Private schools will teach them the latest technology," Itzikowit said. "Another DSA policy that will hurt middle and lower income families the most." Brendan Falk, founder and CEO of Hercules Brendan Falk, founder and CEO of Hercules, an AI app builder, called the AI ban "unfortunate" on Thursday. "This is like banning computers in the 90s or the internet in the 2000s," Falk wrote in a post on X. Gabriel Petersson, cofounder and CEO of Energy Gabriel Petersson, the CEO of an AI-powered productivity app and a former OpenAI researcher, said that banning AI is to him, similar to "banning all computers then giving someone a corporate job." "These kids will be doing their work with assistance of ai if they choose white collar jobs," Petersson said. "Like there is a clear difference in skill in people who grew up with computer versus those that started in high school." Will Hobick, head of design engineering at Rocket Will Hobick, head of design engineering at Rocket, a mortgage platform, called banning AI in schools "completely backwards." "The question isn't whether middle schoolers are going to grow up using AI. They are," said Hobick in a post on X. "The question is whether we teach them how to use it well." "Blocking the technology is easy," Hobick added. "Teaching kids how to use it responsibly is the actual work that the administration has decided they can't do."

item.title: Nissan's AI-powered factory robots can haul 4,000 pounds — and call each other for backup
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.29
Robots can get stuck in traffic, too. Nissan learned that while deploying a fleet of AI-powered robots, called autonomous mobile robots, or AMRs, at its sprawling factory in Smyrna, Tennessee. At one point, the software dispatched two AMRs to the same place at the same time, creating a decidedly futuristic traffic jam. "Of course you wish everything works perfect, out of the box," JS Bolton, Nissan's senior director of manufacturing at the plant, told Business Insider. "But, it doesn't." Teams inside Nissan partnered with software providers and corrected the programming. Now, the automaker says the robots can haul loads weighing thousands of pounds, recharge themselves, and call in another machine if one falls behind. Nissan is completing the first of six deployment phases over the coming months at the plant where it assembles the Rogue, Pathfinder, Murano, and Infiniti QX60. More vehicles are set to come to the factory next year, too. Tim Slate, the plant's director of body and stamping, said the project is Smyrna's largest cost-reduction initiative this year. "This is the top thing on the list," Slate said. Nissan's robots are replacing some forklift trips Nissan's new AMRs are made by OTTO, a company owned by Rockwell Automation. The same bots are found on Ford, GE, Hershey, and Caterpillar plants, too, according to Rockwell's website. Unlike automated carts that follow strips of magnetic tape on factory floors, AMRs use lidar, cameras, and other sensors to navigate around people and obstacles. The largest OTTO model can carry roughly 4,190 pounds and travel at about 4.5 mph. Nissan is using the machines inside Smyrna's body shop, where metal components are welded together to form vehicle bodies. Forklift operators still carry racks of components from truck docks to a deployment area. An AMR then drives underneath a rack, raises its platform about 2.5 inches, and carries the components to a worker who loads them into a robotic production cell. "We really want our technicians to be focused on adding value to the vehicle," Bolton said. "The customer doesn't care how parts get to the assembly line. What they care about is that it's the highest quality on the assembly line." The robots communicate with Nissan's production equipment, allowing them to adjust deliveries in real time. If a robotic cell stops working and no longer consumes parts, for example, an AMR can recognize that the station no longer needs a new delivery. If one machine falls behind on a task — called a "mission" inside the plant — another can step in. The robots themselves have been reliable, Slate said. The harder task has been getting their software to communicate with Nissan's material-flow system and the controllers operating its production equipment. Employees for Powerhouse Controls, the automation systems integration supplier, have been working at the plant around the clock, sometimes seven days a week, as Nissan completes the rollout. Forklift operators remain available to move parts whenever the automated system has a problem. "We can't have downtime," Slate said. Sixty-four workers will move into different jobs Once the rollout is complete, the machines will take over work currently performed by 64 forklift and tug operators. The workers will stay at Nissan, but their current roles will disappear, the company says. Nissan has opened opportunities for those workers to bid for openings elsewhere in the plant, including jobs more directly involved in building vehicles. Some may receive training for positions involving industrial robots and other equipment. "These individuals, frankly, won't have a role," Slate said. "But they will still have a job here." Nissan said it will not backfill its existing material-handling positions, allowing it to reduce overall labor costs. Employees have had mixed reactions. Slate said he notified workers on both shifts about four months before the transition and told them they could begin seeking other positions. "Initially, as you would imagine, it kind of didn't go so well," Slate said. "Initially, all they heard was, 'Our job's not going to be here.'" Some workers remain resistant to the change, he said. Others have embraced it, including a longtime forklift operator who recently stopped Slate in the factory to excitedly share that he was moving to another shop. The automaker says that many of the new positions are better suited for "upward mobility," including, potentially, higher pay. Nissan has previously told Business Insider that its factory technology isn't intended to eliminate jobs. Victor Taylor, Nissan's divisional vice president of manufacturing for the Americas, said that the company wanted to automate "mundane tasks that are really antiquated for a human being to be performing." It's all part of Nissan's turnaround Nissan is under pressure to lower costs as it works through a broader sales turnaround. The company's first-half 2026 sales were up 9.6% compared to the year before, when deliveries dropped by 6.5%. In a separate interview, Chris Reed, Nissan's regional senior vice president of research and development, told Business Insider the company is examining the total cost of producing a vehicle, including supply chain, warranty, development, and labor costs. "We're pushing on everything at the same time," Reed said, including "the number of minutes it takes to build the car." Bolton said making Smyrna more efficient could help the US plant compete for additional vehicle production, particularly as automakers look to manufacture more cars closer to American buyers. "We want to be part of Nissan's recovery," Bolton said. "We see being cost competitive in Smyrna as our contribution to that." Nissan is now studying whether AMRs or automated forklifts could handle components inside Smyrna's stamping operation. It is also considering bringing similar robots into general assembly, where workers install most of a vehicle's parts, with potential projects beginning as soon as 2027. The challenge will be deciding when the technology is sufficiently capable, affordable, and integrable enough to justify the investment. "Any year you don't invest, you're leaving savings on the table," Bolton said. "At the same time, the capability is improving."

item.title: Oura takes step toward IPO with S-1 filing, revealing $1.4 billion in revenue
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.06
Oura just got one step closer to becoming a public company. The smart-ring maker filed its S-1 paperwork on Thursday, a required step on the road to an initial public offering. The filing said Oura pulled in $1.4 billion in revenue and $59 million in net income in the one-year period that ended in June. The company said revenue had grown 74% year-over-year, comparing the first three quarters of fiscal year 2026 to the same period in 2025. Oura also said in the filing that it has "a history of operating losses" and has "only recently achieved profitability," adding "there can be no assurance that we will maintain profitability in any future period." The filing showed Oura incurred losses of $924 million on revenue of $1.21 billion for the nine-month period ended in June. For the same period a year prior, the company's losses were $182.8 million on revenues of $697.6 million. The Oura Ring maker, which plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker OURA, had 5 million paid members as of June, the filing said. The filing lists several risk factors facing the company, as is required in S-1s by the Securities and Exchange Commission. "We have experienced rapid growth in recent years," the risk factors section says. "This rapid growth may not be sustainable or indicative of future performance, and we expect our growth rate to slow over time." The company said current trade tensions and tariffs could increase the cost of some of its products, while broader economic pressure and changes in consumer spending levels could impact its business. The filing also said much of Oura's revenue comes from a "limited number of retail partners." The company said that for the nine months ended in June, its two largest customers accounted for 12% and 10% of its total revenue, respectively. Oura said its business relies on outside AI models, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, and on third-party data centers, adding that disruptions to the data centers could impact the company. It also said there were "legal, regulatory, ethical, security, or reputational risks" associated with AI.

item.title: American just gave its largest Boeing jets a major business class makeover. See how the cabin changed.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.06
American Airlines' largest Boeing widebody plane just got a major makeover. On Wednesday, the airline unveiled its new Flagship business class suites for its 20-strong Boeing 777-300ER fleet. American said it's the most premium-packed jet in the US, with 144 premium seats in total: 70 business-class suites, 44 premium economy seats, and 30 extra-legroom Main Cabin Extra seats. The 777-300ER is the third aircraft type American has fitted with the upgraded Flagship Suite. The cabin debuted on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s in June 2025 and later launched on the Airbus A321XLR in December 2025. Customers experienced the new Flagship interior for the first time on a flight from New York-JFK to Buenos Aires on Wednesday, and it features a lot of new perks compared to the old version. Business-class finally has doors, as well as more storage, more space, and better entertainment. Perhaps most notably, it doesn't have Flagship First, the last of its kind among US carriers. The distinctive cabin will no longer be available for booking from November 19 amid low demand and customer preference for a better business class. American — and the broader airline industry — continue to bet on premium travel as passengers remain willing to pay more for added comforts. Earlier this year, United Airlines announced a new "Elevated" interior for its Boeing 787s, featuring 99 business-class and premium-economy seats. Delta has also announced new cabins for its future Airbus A350-1000s, set to debut in 2027, with premium seats making up 50% of the jet. Business-class seats are highly profitable and account for a significant part of airlines' ticket revenue, helping pad their bottom lines even as some consumers pull back on spending and the conflict in the Middle East drives up fuel prices. In the airline's July earnings call, American chief commercial officer Nat Pieper said that much of that revenue is from affluent customers, saying, "Nearly 60% of our revenue comes from households making $150,000 or more, and so that's demand that's more likely to hold up through economic uncertainty." Here's a closer look at how American is capitalizing on the premium boom, and how its new Flagship Suite compares to the old one. American's previous 777-300ER business class debuted back in 2013. The old version, pictured, had 52 seats and was a major upgrade for its time. It differed from the unpopular 2×2×2 and 2×3×2 layouts American had installed on other Boeing widebodies, which forced window-seat flyers to crawl over their neighbors to access the aisle, while some were stuck in middle seats. It also offered better seatback screens, a more comfortable and private sleeping setup, and a walk-up snack bar, stocked with drinks, fruit, chips, and cookies. The latter will remain available in American's new 777-300ER business class. The new Flagship Business maintains a 1×2×1 layout. The configuration, pictured in the bottom image, will include one seat angled in by the window and two in the middle angled toward each other, with a privacy divider between them. Every passenger will retain direct aisle access. The new seats, which span 19 rows, are made by Elevate Aircraft Seating (formerly Adient Aerospace) and are also used on American's 787s. The top photo is the old version, which had 52 seats — 18 fewer than the new Flagship. It also now features ever-popular sliding doors. Among the most highly requested perks from premium travelers are sliding doors. American's old version didn't have the door but instead had a large curved wing for privacy. The new door is also fully certified and doesn't need to be locked open, as was the case with the airline's A321XLR doors at launch. Those have since been approved by the Federal Aviation Administration. To pack in 70 business-class seats, American shaved an inch of legroom. According to the airline seating information website SeatMaps, the previous 777 business class, pictured, had one more inch of legroom, 42 inches now versus 43 before — a negligible difference. "When retrofitting any aircraft, we utilize the space available to be able to offer a variety of products for customers to choose from," an American spokesperson told Business Insider. There are now more storage and power ports. Both versions have a cubby and nooks, but American said the new version, pictured right, offers more storage space than the previous one (left), including a dedicated drink surface, shelves, and a laptop slot. Both versions offer charging via USB-A and AC ports, but the new one also includes wireless charging and USB-C. The seatback screen is also a few inches wider. All seatback screens in business class feature 17.5-inch 4K displays with Bluetooth — both significant upgrades from the previous screens. There's also a remote, but it isn't touchscreen. The seat also has a "Do Not Disturb" mode, adjustable ambient lighting, and a large tray table. There is a patented chaise lounge mode. American's unique chaise-lounge mode, which is also on the 787, allows passengers to sit upright and lean against the suite shell with their legs stretched out onto the lie-flat bed, like they're lounging on a beach chair. A patented second seatbelt keeps them secure in this position. Flagship Preferred Suites replace Flagship First. The eight Flagship First suites, complete with a swivel chair that creates a small office, are now Flagship Preferred: eight oversized suites with an ottoman that accommodates an additional passenger, allowing families to dine or socialize together, or colleagues to meet. The special nook, which takes advantage of the extra space in the bulkhead rows, is also on the 787s. Passengers can book the 777 Preferred at no additional fee, though American may monetize it in the future, as other carriers have. For example, United's similar Polaris Studio starts at $499 to add. Here's what Flagship First looked like. Flagship Business gets access to the lounge. Flagship travelers get priority check-in, boarding, security, and baggage handling, as well as access to the Flagship lounge, where available. Onboard meals are chef-curated, and the plane is stocked with premium wines and spirits. Flyers also get an amenity kit, and the linens include a cool-touch dual-sided pillow, a blanket, and a mattress pad. AAdvantage loyalty members also get access to free high-speed WiFi. The jet also includes a new premium economy cabin. The 44 upgraded premium economy seats — up from 28 — offer better privacy and space, along with elevated meals, Bluetooth connectivity, water bottle storage, wireless charging, USB-C and AC power ports, adjustable headrests, and calf and foot rests. It's considered the middle-ground in terms of price and comfort between business class and coach. Still, the 777 is so wide that American can fit eight across, meaning there are two middle seats per row. Economy was also retrofitted. American revamped the old coach and extra legroom seats with better padding, inflight entertainment, and Bluetooth connectivity. It maintains its 10-abreast seating configuration, with 216 seats in total: 186 in Main Cabin and 30 in Main Cabin Extra. Overall, the plane has 330 seats — the previous setup had 304. American's retrofitted 777-300ER will fly to five cities. American has rapidly expanded its international network to cash in on long-haul premium demand — cabins that sell for thousands of dollars to destinations across Europe, Asia, and beyond. The 777-300ER's international routes include London, Tokyo, São Paulo, Buenos Aires, and Sydney.

item.title: Emirates is bringing one of business travelers' favorite features to its premium economy cabins
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.04
For years, privacy on planes was reserved for the wealthiest travelers. Now that's changing. Emirates unveiled a new premium-economy seat on Thursday, with a unique privacy screen. As well as being more private, the new seat is easier to recline and raise the legrest with electric controls. Plus, it reclines in a cradle position, which avoids intruding on the passenger behind. While Japan Airlines was the first to introduce electric controls in premium economy, Emirates' new seat also uses them to control the privacy divider, which extends to the full height of the seat. Wealthy travelers have grown more accustomed to privacy since Emirates first introduced a sliding door to its first-class suites in 2003. In the years since, they've become essentially de rigueur in business class. However, premium economy passengers have typically had little to separate them from their neighbors. Many premium-economy cabins lack any privacy screens, instead using a small panel that extends from the headrest. United Airlines introduced a divider in its Premium Plus cabin last year, although it does not extend to the seat's full height. While electric controls can make life easier for passengers, they are at a higher risk of malfunctioning than manual controls, increasing maintenance costs. Emirates' new seat also includes the U-Dream headrest that it revealed for the economy cabin at July's Farnborough Airshow. It features two side wings that fold down and inward. "The U-Dream changes the game if the person wants to sleep — by supporting the neck in full," Emirates President Tim Clark said in the press release. "No more neck pillows needed." Business Insider tried the new headrest at Farnborough and found it to be a genuine game changer. Emirates' new premium-economy seats also feature wireless charging, and a tray table with an integrated phone holder — if you need a second screen in addition to the 13.3-inch 4K one on the seatback. Emirates did not say when the new seat will debut, other than it being "on board soon," nor which routes would see it first. It will be available on newly delivered Airbus A350 airplanes. They have 28 premium-economy seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. The seats are 20 inches wide and have a pitch of 39 inches — the distance between the same spot on one seat and that of the row behind. Emirates was relatively late to the premium-economy trend, first adding the cabin to its flagship Airbus A380 aircraft in early 2021. The cabin has become especially popular since the pandemic. With travelers willing to spend extra money for more luxury, premium economy bridges the gap to business class.

item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.03
The country's largest colleges aren't always a single enormous campus packed with students. From giant historic flagships to statewide community colleges, the biggest school in each state can look very different. But those who prefer larger colleges gain access to more majors, extracurriculars, and a diverse student body. Business Insider compiled a list of every state's largest college using provisional fall 2024 data from the Department of Education's Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS). To better reflect the size of colleges' in-person student populations, we subtracted students enrolled exclusively online from each institution's total enrollment number. We then ranked schools using that adjusted figure. Students taking a mix of online and in-person classes remained in the count. This means online-only or online-heavy institutions, such as the University of Maryland Global Campus, did not necessarily rank first, despite having overall larger student populations than other institutions in their states. Some of the colleges in this ranking encompass more than one physical campus. Depending on the institution, the data may cover one campus or several campuses and locations reported together. Where IPEDS specifies a campus, that name is included in the slide description. Because the data is provisional, they're not necessarily an exact final count of how many students attended that fall. item.title: OpenAI's ad for its latest model looks straight out of the movie 'WALL-E' — and people have thoughts
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.59
At this point, there's hardly any reason to get off the couch. OpenAI released a demonstration video for its new Astra model on Thursday. In the clip, people sit or pace before a large screen, barking orders at the model, which heeds their demands — including requests to list furniture on eBay and order takeout — almost instantly. The futuristic video, which so far has more than 75 million views on X, sparked a spirited online debate: How much is too much automation? And how long until humanity starts to resemble the sedentary space people from "WALL-E?" "Give humans nothing to do, nothing to build, nothing to struggle for long enough, and Idiocracy stops looking like satire and starts looking like a roadmap," one user wrote on X. OpenAI's new model The ChatGPT maker called Astra "the world's most intelligent and aligned model" in a press release on Thursday. OpenAI said it applied lessons from what it called the "Hugging Face incident," in which rogue agents hacked into the platform's servers during a test, to make Astra safer. By Friday, some users on X were proudly displaying highly detailed 3D scenes created on Blender via prompts on Astra. GPT-6 Astra vs Fable 5.1 in Blender… The gap in visual quality is actually crazy 👀 AI is getting dangerously good at turning prompts into fully built 3D scenes. Which one would you pick? pic.twitter.com/SIFmpzlEzu Other users posted clips from video games they designed using the new model. Users said the games were easy to create and highly steerable. Astra (GPT-6) is here!!! I've had early access and tested it like crazy with things like games, code, writing, browser control, presentations and general knowledge work. This is the best model I've ever used. Period. (Incredible demos below in this thread ⬇️) Here's my take… pic.twitter.com/t1CMMSBelQ A dystopian future Astra quickly drew comparisons to various movies in which characters rely on AI to the point of being unable to live without it. Some comparisons were flattering — like Jarvis, Iron Man's digital companion who controls his armor and occasionally delivers dry jokes. Other people, though, said that with models like Astra, it was only a matter of time before humanity regressed into a slothful, inert species with no reason to move, travel, or work. Thanks. Even more lazy people now. Its going to be like the people from WALL-E soon pic.twitter.com/KVsDVJB5UH In "WALL-E," the 2008 Pixar classic, humanity abandoned Earth after it became filled with garbage. They left the planet aboard a giant spaceship, and 700 years later, the population evolved into obese screen-watchers who got their nutrition through straws. "You know, survival, longevity, health, food, regenerative food, all that stuff," the film's director, Andrew Stanton, told NPR in 2008 when it first came out. "So what's the point of living? And so it was like this hellacious, perpetual vacation." Users on X also compared the technology to the 2013 film "Her," directed by Spike Jonze, in which the main character, played by Joaquin Phoenix, falls in love with an AI companion before discovering that it's also in love with more than 600 other people.

item.title: Nvidia has built a $99 billion equity portfolio from almost scratch in 2 years
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.38
Nvidia has built a nearly $100 billion equity portfolio from virtually scratch in just two years by investing in other tech companies. The AI chipmaker, led by CEO Jensen Huang, held $99 billion in equity investments as of July 26, according to its latest earnings report. That included roughly $48 billion in publicly traded stocks and other marketable securities, $48 billion in shares of private companies and other non-marketable securities, and $3 billion in equity-method investments. Its equity portfolio surged 14-fold in a year from about $7 billion last summer, and 45-fold from $2.2 billion two summers ago. The company also reported a further $25 billion in equity investment commitments as of July 26. Nvidia's quarterly portfolio disclosure offered a glimpse at its public US stock portfolio as of June 30. It held a $30 billion stake in Intel, a $21 billion position in SpaceX, and investments in CoreWeave, Coherent, Synopsys, and Nokia, each worth between $2 billion and $5 billion. The huge increase in Nvidia's equity holdings has vaulted it into the ranks of the biggest tech investors. It still trails the likes of Alphabet, which had a $232 billion equity portfolio at the end of June, including $94 billion of SpaceX shares following its IPO in June. Nvidia stock has rocketed from below $15 at the start of 2023 to $228 at Thursday's close. That 15-fold increase in under three years has catapulted its market capitalization to $5.5 trillion, making it the world's most valuable company. The chipmaker has become the premier enabler of the AI boom by providing the types of semiconductors needed to power the nascent technology, financing the AI infrastructure buildout, and investing in its AI peers. A Nvidia spokesperson pointed Business Insider to finance chief Colette Kress, saying on the company's latest earnings call that frontier AI labs' ability to improve their products, attract more users, and generate more revenue was being "limited by compute," so Nvidia was "needed to help power this flywheel" and had thus invested almost $50 billion in them. In its latest earnings report, Nvidia said that it makes equity investments to "enhance our growth opportunities, cultivate our ecosystem, and strengthen our competitive position." However, Michael Burry of "The Big Short" fame has said Nvidia is "overreaching" in its efforts to juice its growth by financing and investing in customers of its chips. Similarly, former "Shark Tank" investor Mark Cuban has said it's "truly scary" how reliant the AI boom is on Nvidia "funding everyone and anyone."

item.title: Dude Perfect's first CEO is out after disagreeing with the board about the company's next phase
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.34
YouTube sports collective Dude Perfect is losing its first CEO, Andrew Yaffe, after about two years in the role, a company rep confirmed. Patrick Hurley, a principal at BP Capital Fund Advisors and an advisor to Dude Perfect, will serve as interim CEO. The company has hired a firm to begin the search for a permanent chief executive. A joint statement from the company's board and Yaffe said the change was a mutual decision. "After two years of strong growth, Andrew and the Board have decided that now is the right time for new leadership at Dude Perfect. As the social media landscape continues to evolve, they developed different perspectives on the company's next phase and the best path forward," it said. The statement said that the company had grown revenue significantly since Yaffe joined, driven by partnerships with State Farm, Disney, and others, and expanded through its live tour and other initiatives. The joint statement came via prominent publicist Matthew Hiltzik, who's represented a wide range of public figures and is known for handling crisis PR situations, though his work goes beyond that. In addition to working with Dude Perfect over the years, he represents fellow creator MrBeast. Yaffe, a former NBA exec, said in a LinkedIn post that he and Dude Perfect "decided to go our separate ways." "I'm so proud of what we built together and how much progress we were able to make in less than 24 months, adding world-class talent to our team, defining a mission to Inspire Play and having clear business results and momentum to show for it," he said. Axios first reported the news of Yaffe's departure. Texas-based Dude Perfect, founded in 2009 by five college roommates, is one of the few creator-led companies to receive significant outside funding, raising over $100 million in early 2024 from Highmount Capital. The five Dudes — Garrett Hilbert, Tyler Toney, Cody Jones, Coby Cotton, and Cory Cotton — are known for their wholesome, kid-friendly content featuring sports tricks. Based in Frisco, Texas, the company has grown into a sprawling enterprise with more than 62 million YouTube subscribers, merch sales, and a 22-city live tour. It's also announced plans to open a theme park, but hasn't shared any recent updates. Earlier this year, Dude Perfect teamed up with Good Good, the YouTube golf collective, to tap each other's audiences through cobranded merch and live events. Good Good also shook up its leadership this week, with its CEO and president exiting on Wednesday amid backlash from a controversial ad with its former partner, Callaway, that critics said promoted violence against women. Good Good lost retail and merchandise partnerships as part of the fallout. Hiltzik declined to comment on the status of Dude Perfect's Good Good partnership.

item.title: OpenAI does a victory lap for its new AI model: 'Welcome to the AGI era'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.17
OpenAI says that its new model has reached the AI industry's most sought-after milestone. "Welcome to the AGI era," Greg Brockman, the company's president, said at the end of a press call announcing the arrival of OpenAI's Astra model on Thursday. AGI stands for artificial general intelligence, a fuzzy concept that nonetheless has become a core goal for AI development. OpenAI defines it as "highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work." The company pitched Astra as a major research breakthrough and a shift in what's possible to delegate to AI. It's rolling out to customers this week. Brockman has described reaching AGI as a gradual process. On the Thursday call, he said that in the future, he thinks people will look back and think AGI was created "about this time, and I think it might be about this model." "For me personally, I do think we're there," he said. GPT-6 Astra comes about a year after OpenAI launched its GPT-5 model family and about two months after its most recent upgrades, dubbed GPT-5.6. The company called Astra "the world's most intelligent and aligned model," and a "step change in professional work." The model will also improve ChatGPT's "computer use" abilities, the company said. OpenAI employees told Business Insider last month that those tools — which run tasks autonomously on a user's desktop computer or internet browser — have reached an inflection point. The blog post said Astra can fill out forms, format documents, schedule appointments, and operate software. Although successful "computer use" AI agents have been a long-standing goal of OpenAI and other tech giants, the technology is tricky because there's such a wide variety in people's desktop work, and so far, the tools have been fairly slow. "Anything you can do on a computer, Astra can do for you. Fast," OpenAI wrote on X. OpenAI previously said it delayed Astra's release until September after identifying improvements in its cybersecurity capabilities. The company wrote earlier this week that it needed to ensure Astra's safeguards block its use by bad actors for hacking and that the model itself is aligned to do what's asked of it. Like Brockman, other tech leaders have held up AGI as a goal. Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis said at the company's May conference that he expected AGI to arrive as soon as 2030, adding that humanity is standing "on the foothills of the singularity." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, for his part, told the Sources podcast in a recent appearance that AGI is, at best, "a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it's like an irrelevant marketing term." item.title: Volkswagen plans 50,000 more job cuts amid biggest overhaul in its history
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.80
Volkswagen plans to cut roughly 50,000 more jobs worldwide. On Thursday, the company's supervisory board approved its "Future Plan 2030," a 12-part restructuring effort that Volkswagen calls the "most extensive transformation program" in its history. Volkswagen said a "fundamental adjustment" of its global workforce — including management roles — will be necessary beyond its existing cost-cutting programs. It did not say where the positions would be eliminated, when the reductions would happen, or whether they would come through layoffs, buyouts, or attrition. The job cuts are one piece of a much broader reset. Volkswagen plans to halve its model portfolio by 2035 and reduce the complexity of its vehicle offerings by about 75%. It also aims to sell about 9 million vehicles annually and reach a 9% operating margin by 2030. That will mean fewer models and variants, higher volumes for the cars it keeps, and lower costs across its sprawling group of brands, which includes Volkswagen, Audi, Porsche, Škoda, Seat, Cupra, Bentley, and Lamborghini. The company has been facing steep competition from lower-cost Chinese automakers, especially on its home turf in Europe. The expensive transition to electric vehicle development, US automotive tariffs, and high energy prices are not helping either. It's part of a larger trend in the auto industry: Car companies have gone through a decluttering era as they try to reduce costs as they face the compounding headwinds. Volkswagen is one of the most dramatic examples. On Thursday, the automaker said its European factories have capacity for more than 500,000 vehicles beyond current demand. That leaves the future production plans for four German factories — Emden, Zwickau, Hanover, and Neckarsulm — uncertain from 2031 through 2034. Volkswagen said it is considering alternative uses for the plants. The new workforce reduction comes on top of existing programs. In 2024, Volkswagen AG agreed with labor representatives to cut more than 35,000 jobs at its German sites by 2030. Volkswagen didn't immediately respond to Business Insider's questions about how its new global target overlaps with those earlier planned reductions.

item.title: Inside the Han Kuang — how Taiwan prepares for the world's most consequential war
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.88
Caught between two superpowers, Taiwan stands to be the world's most dangerous flash point. The island democracy of 23.2 million people knows its precarious position. For the last four decades, the global semiconductor hub has conducted annual military drills focused on staving off a cross-strait invasion by Beijing, which considers the island part of its territory and refuses to rule out a seizure by military force. The Han Kuang exercises, originally meant to display Taiwan's mettle to mainland China and the world, are quickly taking on a new form. Taipei is now more keen to use the drills as a realistic stress test for its outnumbered forces and civilian institutions. Force-on-force combat and audacious beach landings that characterized previous Han Kuangs have given way to an emphasis on smaller skirmishes, logistics missions, and ambush setups. The change comes as a proverbial, though hypothetical, deadline for Taiwan looms: China's Xi Jinping has ordered his country's troops to be ready for military action by 2027. While analysts around the world don't see how Beijing could pull off an invasion by then, the threat remains. Business Insider attended over a dozen drills during the 42nd edition of the Han Kuang, which ran for 10 days and nine nights in August. The exercises show how the island has been preparing for what its likeliest scenarios, from decapitation strikes to sabotage to urban warfare, with an arsenal of American, European, and domestic weaponry. All the while, the US — widely regarded as Taiwan's main hope of defeating a full-on Chinese attack — has kept a close watch, quietly sending advisors to observe. Check out our coverage of Han Kuang 2026, Taiwan's rehearsal of what could be the most consequential battle of the modern age.

item.title: I've been on over 55 cruises. Here are 7 of the biggest mistakes I see cruisers make.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.81
I've traveled all over the world, and cruising continues to be one of the easiest ways to visit new places. You can unpack once while waking up in a new destination every day, all while having dining and entertainment just steps from your cabin. But planning a cruise can be more complicated than you might anticipate. Between booking flights to the departure city, choosing a cabin, making reservations, and planning your time ashore, there are plenty of decisions that can make or break your vacation. After more than 55 cruises, I feel like I see cruisers making the same avoidable mistakes. Fortunately, I've learned that a little preparation can make all the difference in preventing unnecessary stress. Here are the seven biggest mistakes I see cruisers make — and what I recommend doing instead. Booking flights too close to embarkation or disembarkation Choosing the wrong flights is one of the biggest mistakes I see cruisers make. If you're flying to your departure port, it's crucial to book flights that will leave enough time for potential disruptions. It's the golden rule of cruising to arrive at least one day before embarkation in case your flight is delayed or canceled. For an international cruise, I recommend arriving at least two days early, if not more. When possible, I also book a nonstop flight to reduce the chance of disruptions. Otherwise, if you don't reach the cruise port in time, the ship can leave without you. You should also be cautious when booking a flight home. Although your ship might dock at 7 a.m., that doesn't mean you should book an early-morning return flight. Disembarkation can take longer than expected with long lines, luggage collection, and immigration. For the trip home, a late afternoon or evening flight can provide breathing room and help prevent a stressful end to your vacation. Reserving a cabin without looking at the deck plans When booking a cruise, you'll find many different cabin categories and locations. You might not think twice about your room's location, but a bad experience can dampen your entire cruise. Some cabins can be especially noisy, such as those near the elevators, under the pool deck, or close to the bars. If you're a light sleeper, this extra noise can make it difficult to get enough rest each night. Similarly, if you're prone to motion sickness, a cabin at the front of the ship might make you feel extra queasy during rough seas. Before choosing a cruise cabin, review your ship's deck plans to find the best location that minimizes noise and motion. I recommend selecting a midship stateroom with other cabins nearby, including the decks directly above and below it. Bringing prohibited items on board Another common mistake I see cruisers make is packing items that aren't allowed on the ship. Cruise lines' websites usually have a long list of prohibited items due to safety regulations, legal restrictions, and fire hazards. Because of these strict rules, you'll want to leave your weapons, irons, and steamers at home. If you forget, your item(s) may be confiscated before disembarkation. In more serious cases, a cruise line can even prevent you from boarding the ship. In this way, it's a good idea to review your cruise line's specific list of prohibited items before packing. Missing out on amenities you've already paid for Although there are plenty of ways to spend extra money on board, your cruise fare often covers more than you might realize. In fact, I've seen many cruisers assume certain restaurants or onboard thrills cost extra when they're actually complimentary. Last summer, after I tried the Ultimate Abyss dry slide on Wonder of the Seas, another passenger approached me and asked how much it cost. When I told her it was free, she was shocked! With so much to see and do on board, it can be difficult to keep track of which experiences are included and which cost extra. Before boarding, review the ship's included dining venues, amenities, and attractions, so you know what you've already paid for. Don't assume something costs extra without checking first — this info is usually available in the cruise line's app or on the daily schedule. Forgetting to make reservations Some onboard experiences require reservations, but if you wait until embarkation day, you might be left with few options. Specialty restaurants can be especially likely to fill up, with the most popular dining times being booked first. Depending on the ship, reservations might also be required for headliner shows and productions. For example, Royal Caribbean's biggest vessels often ask guests to reserve seats for its ice-skating spectacles, AquaTheatre shows, and Broadway-style performances. Before sailing, check the cruise planner or app to reserve specialty dining and entertainment. If booking isn't available beforehand, make reservations as soon as you can on embarkation day. This gives you the best chance of securing times that fit your vacation schedule. Cutting it too close when returning to the ship Cruise ships operate on strict schedules, so the all-aboard time is non-negotiable. Cruisers exploring independently are responsible for returning on time, and those seen racing back to the ship because they're late are often called "pier runners." I've seen many pier runners over the years, including two people who were left behind in Prince Edward Island. After repeatedly paging for the missing cruisers and waiting more than 40 minutes past the all-aboard time, our ship eventually set sail. In a scene that felt straight out of a movie, the two late passengers appeared on the pier moments after we pulled away. To avoid being left behind, I recommend returning to the port about an hour before the all-aboard time. This leaves a buffer for traffic or unexpected delays — and you can still explore the port area or terminal before boarding. I also save the port agent's contact information provided by the cruise line in case of an emergency. Not having a disembarkation plan It's easy to overlook disembarkation when putting together a cruise, but not having a plan can turn your final morning into a headache. When I disembarked from a Mediterranean cruise in Ravenna, Italy, some passengers waited in the heat for more than two hours because there were very few taxis available. Thankfully, I had researched the port and arranged our transportation in advance for the two-hour drive to Venice. Before your cruise, research what to expect at the disembarkation port and arrange transportation in advance. I prefer booking disembarkation tours with airport drop-offs through the cruise line, as they're convenient and don't add stress to the end of my vacation.

item.title: Is Germany's economic slump finally over?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.68
The German economy is showing tentative signs of recovery after a prolonged period of gloom. Europe's largest economy is on track for its strongest GDP growth since 2022, while business sentiment is finally trending upwards again after a lengthy spell in the doldrums. The country's official statistics office reported last week that the economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026, beating estimates and building on robust figures for the previous two quarters. Several others have revised their forecasts upwards. The Ifo Institute, Kiel Institute for the World Economy and the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research are all now predicting growth of 1.3% or more for 2026. Meanwhile, the Ifo business climate index — a key barometer of the country's corporate mood — returned its highest reading in a year for August. "It's more than a flash in the pan," Clemens Fuest, president of the Ifo Institute, told DW. "It could be a recovery." "The momentum is positive and the economy has shown a better-than-feared level of resilience," said Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro research. However, he cautioned against too much cheer, saying some of the economy's fundamental problems remain. "In order to really transform this into a longer-term recovery story, we still need more," he said. Where has the good news come from? The positive figures come as negative headlines related to Germany's economy continue to stack up. Volkswagen, one of the country's most iconic companies, is in the midst of a bitter downsizing — reflecting a wider restructuring across the country in the face of competition from China and other global headwinds. This summer, record low water levels on key German waterways such as the Rhine and Danube significantly disrupted trade and economic activity while the war in Iran continues to drive energy prices upwards. Yet part of the reason for the upturn relates to how the German economy has handled some of those challenges, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the Iran war. Germany's exports and industrial base have powered GDP growth, with new orders increasing for the third month in a row, leading to the strongest production growth since early 2022. The VDMA, which represents the German mechanical and plant engineering sector, reported a 2% increase in foreign orders for July year-on-year. Brzeski told DW that many German manufacturing firms, especially in energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals, have benefited from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. They have increased orders and taken some market share from Asian suppliers who were more severely dependent on Middle Eastern oil. "There was a bit of a rechanneling of industrial orders away from Asia to Europe and Germany," he said. The German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action itself identified this factor in its August statement, saying Asian rivals "were more affected by price increases and supply bottlenecks." It said that the multiple shocks of recent years have led German companies to diversify supply chains. "Many companies have altered their transport logistics in recent years, are maintaining larger stocks, and are using a variety of transport routes in order to make their supply chains more resilient," it added. Can the German government take some credit? Analysts also think Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government deserves some credit for the turnaround, despite it hitting historic levels of unpopularity in 2026. "It's driven by government demand and debt-financed spending, particularly in defense," said Fuest. The government's economic plans are built around a €500 billion ($580 billion) infrastructure investment drive, a massive increase in defense spending and a major reform proposal aimed at boosting competitiveness. It has also introduced some energy price relief measures and a €10 billion tax relief plan for lower-income households. "Companies are more optimistic and a big part has to be the stimulus," said Brzeski. "It is gradually reaching the economy." Germany's structural problems remain Despite the positive data, many of the issues which have dogged the German economy in recent years remain. The recent uptick is driven by export demand, with practically no increase in domestic demand. According to the Federal Statistical Office, public and private consumption spending was flat, while investment declined. "Even though everyone is happy that we have some positive news, we need to watch out and not fall into the trap of thinking that now 'everything is fine,'" said Brzeski, noting that the factors undermining German competitiveness persist. "Chinese competition is still there," he said. "The long loss in international competitiveness in the automotive industry and other industries is still here," he added, stressing that these structural challenges would be difficult to alter or reverse. Tentative optimism among Germany's businesses Yet the positive sentiment remains. Indicators for the third quarter of 2026 suggest significant optimism among business leaders about the future, while overall German growth is now on track for a 1.2% increase for 2026. That puts it ahead of other European countries such as France, the UK and the Netherlands. In the wake of the war in Ukraine, Germany's economy fell into a sustained slump from which it has struggled to emerge since 2022. While other economies showed signs of recovery, Germany remained in the doldrums. For some analysts, the recent positive data reflects a sense that things had reached a natural "bottoming out" and that a return to growth was inevitable. "It could hardly have gotten much worse," said Brzeski. "We're bouncing back from low levels. This is not wirtschaftswunder ["economic miracle"] 3.0, we have to keep that in mind." He also thinks part of the optimism is related to corporate Germany finally accepting some harsh truths about how it had fallen behind in key areas such as innovation and digitalization, and belatedly trying to improve. "They realize they simply have to embrace technological change, AI and so on, and have to start investing," he said. "They are no longer waiting for what's happening in Berlin in terms of reform packages; it's a question of survival." For Fuest, the data suggests Germany's "industrial core" remains intact. He said three-quarters of German manufacturing companies are still expanding, but warns that the recovery will be short-lived unless bigger change follows. "It is urgent to allow for structural change and to find new areas where German companies have competitive advantages," he said. Edited by: Rob Mudge

item.title: Can communities be proteced from melting glaciers?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.17
High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall. The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released. Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is known as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Blatten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods. How much is climate change to blame? The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists. Levan Tielidze, research fellow in glacial geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, said the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact." "As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream." Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucasus Mountains of North Ossetia in Russia. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24 kilometers (15 miles) and killed around 125 people. "The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," said Tielidze. Meanwhile, the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability. Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century. For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches." "These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added. Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s. The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event. However, the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain. The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometers, noted Tielidze. "These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he said, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change. Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts? The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blatten resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse. But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, said Tielidze. "In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said. "We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings." For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added. Chapagain said the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems. However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal." "What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group cocoordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement. A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures. "We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt." Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Berlin: BER Airport Terminal 1 reopened after security scare
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.08
Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) was reopened on Thursday evening following an earlier evacuation due to a security scare. "The police operation has ended," said an airport spokeswoman. Federal police, responsible for transportation security in Germany, had evacuated BER Terminal 1 at around 5:45 p.m. after a woman reportedly told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance in her luggage. "A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the police spokesperson told the dpa news agency. Police then gave the all-clear at around 8:45 p.m. and confirmed that nobody had been in danger at any point. Police initially provided no information as to the nature of the substance in question, with analysis results expected in the coming days. Berlin: BER operations remain restricted Despite the all-clear, operations at BER remained restricted on Thursday evening. "Due to the police operation, we will still be experiencing delays and some cancelations until the end of the day," said the airport spokeswoman. She advised travelers to double-check the status of their flight before arriving at BER and to keep an eye on the boards while at the airport. "Flights were not stopped," she insisted, emphasizing that there were only delays. "Regular operations will resume on Friday." What did the airport say about departures and arrivals? The airport had confirmed the incident itself earlier on Thursday but said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land. Passenger processing was "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," a spokesperson said. Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website. An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2. Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains. BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year. The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal.
