Edited by: Zac Crellin, Dmytro Hubenko

item.title: South Africa airline behind viral stadium flyby scraps repeat display
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.79
South African aviation authorities are reviewing a low-altitude flyover by two Airlink passenger planes at an international rugby match in Cape Town last weekend. The regional airline, meanwhile, said it had canceled another flypast scheduled for Saturday's rugby test between South Africa and New Zealand in Johannesburg this weekend, citing unfavorable weather. In a statement, the South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said it was carrying out a "compliance verification" of the August 29 flyover at Cape Town's DHL stadium to ensure "all safety protocols were adhered to by the crew." Footage of the flyby, showing two planes in formation passing over the crowd, was widely shared on social media and prompted discussion about potential safety risks. According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, the lead aircraft passed less than 15 meters (50 feet) above the top of the packed stadium. What did SACAA and Airlink say? The SACAA said it was analyzing flight data provided by Airlink and would go over additional information requested from the carrier before issuing a report. The regulator said the airline had made applications for the flyovers, which were approved in line with the requirements for special air events. Airlink, for its part, said the maneuver had been carefully planned and rehearsed, with safety being "the first consideration at every stage of the process." It said each aircraft had three senior captains on board with a combined 75,000 hours of flying experience. Nevertheless, it also recognized what it described as the "valid questions and concerns." Airlink Chief Executive de Villiers Engelbrecht said the decision had been made to withdraw plans for this weekend's stadium flypast in Johannesburg because "the forecast weather points to unfavorable conditions for a safe formation flyby." A history of flybys in rugby Stadium flybys have long been tradition at major rugby matches in South Africa, dating back to the 1995 Rugby World Cup final in Johannesburg, when a Boeing 747 swept overhead before the Springboks faced the All Blacks. The SACAA said in a statement that South Africa "is ranked seventh globally and first in Africa for our aviation safety standards by the International Civil Aviation Organization." There have been no fatal accidents in its commercial airline operations space for over four decades, it added. Edited by: Louis Oelofse If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.33
New King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance to Norway's consititution in the parliament in Oslo on Tuesday, following him succeeding his father Harald V, who died last week. This follows a day after Harald's coffin was taken to the chapel of the royal palace, where it will remain for the public to pay their last respects until a funeral on September 9. What happened in the parliamentary ceremony? Haakon was driven the short distance from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament in Oslo. House speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession before the new constitutional monarch took the oath. "I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in according with its constitution and laws, so help me god, the almighty and omniscient," the 53-year-old said. Queen Mette-Marit skips event amid complications following lung transplant Ahead of he ceremony, the palace said that Haakon's wife Queen Mette-Marit would not be attending. She had made her first public appearance since assuming the title on Monday in the coffin procession but is recovering after a lung transplant in June. In a statement, the palace quoted Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo's University Hospital, as saying that complications following a transplant are not uncommon and that Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday. "As a result, the Queen must remain under observation throughout the day. Unfortunately, the Queen will therefore be unable to attend the swearing-in ceremony at the Storting today," he said. What's the role of Norway's largely symbolic monarchy? Norway's royal family can trace its roots bak to the ninth century. When the country regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters supported the idea of reinstating a largely symbolic constitutional monarchy in a plebiscite. Most political power lies with the elected government and parliament, but Norway's royals retain a predominantly soft power role in diplomacy and promoting the country around the world. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first. Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

item.title: Malaysia's middle path between China and US faces new tests
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.29
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has spent much of his time in office insisting that Kuala Lumpur will not be forced to choose between the United States and China. But two sets of comments last month have raised questions about how sustainable that position is as rivalry between the two superpowers increasingly spills into Southeast Asia. "I see Taiwan as part of China, period," he said in an interview with news outlet Al Jazeera that aired on August 16. Beijing considers democratically governed Taiwan part of its territory. While Chinese leaders say they favor "peaceful reunification," they have never ruled out using force to bring the island under Beijing's control. More controversially, Anwar appeared to accept Beijing's argument that force could be necessary. "If one province decides to break away. Do we use force? I think I will, [to] protect the sanctity and unity of the nation," he said. Regional concerns The comments drew an enthusiastic response from Beijing, while Taiwan's Foreign Ministry accused Anwar of effectively legitimizing the use of force against the islandand warned that his "one-sided support for China could negatively impact Taiwanese businesses' confidence in investing in Malaysia," including in the country's strategically important semiconductor sector. Two days after his comments on Taiwan aired, Anwar argued that Malaysia should strengthen its defenses in Sabah, citing the expansion of US-backed military facilities on the nearby Philippine island of Balabac. The Philippines is upgrading facilities on Balabac, roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Malaysian islands of Banggi and Balambangan. Balabac was one of four additional locations added in 2023 to the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, which allows US forces to access designated Philippine military facilities, construct infrastructure and pre-position equipment. Taken together, Anwar's comments raised concerns that Malaysia is growing warmer toward Beijing while becoming more suspicious of Washington's military footprint in the region. A fundamental realignment? Kuala Lumpur has also been one of the region's strongest critics of Israel's actions in Gaza. Anwar has repeatedly accused the United States and European governments of hypocrisy and double standards for championing democracy and international law while failing, in his view, to hold Israel sufficiently accountable. But Malaysia experts warn against interpreting Anwar's rhetoric as evidence of a fundamental strategic realignment. "Malaysia still maintains very good relations with the US and other Western countries," Ngeow Chow Bing, director of the Institute of China Studies at Universiti Malaya, told DW. Those ties may sometimes be less visible than Anwar's increasingly warm public rhetoric towards Beijing, Bing said, but the underlying relationship remains strong. "It is certainly true that the space for maintaining its traditional balancing act between China and the US is narrower than before, but that space remains, and Malaysia will continue to operate within it," Bing added. A shift in tone, not strategy Anwar's comments about the Philippine military buildup are much more about an ongoing territorial dispute between Kuala Lumpur and Manila, Chee Meng Tan, assistant professor at the University of Nottingham Malaysia, told DW. The Philippines maintains a territorial claim over Sabah, which became part of Malaysia when the federation was formed in 1963. Malaysia rejects the claim and regards its sovereignty over the state as indisputable. Those tensions resurface regularly, and in August Kuala Lumpur lodged a fresh objection with the United Nations over a Philippine submission about its continental shelf. "A neighbor that claims part of your territory is building a military base 20 minutes offshore — any government would react," said Tan. Anwar called for the strengthening of Malaysia's own defenses, not for Chinese help, "and he went out of his way to say relations with Manila remain good," Tan added. Anwar also sought to lower the temperature over Taiwan after his initial comments. Speaking to Malaysian media after the event, he stressed that Kuala Lumpur wanted a peaceful resolution to cross-strait tensions and insisted that Malaysia's position had not changed. Malaysia has formally followed a "One China" policy since establishing diplomatic relations with Beijing in 1974. Chinese state media quickly interpreted Anwar's remarks through Beijing's preferred terminology, with Xinhua reporting that the Malaysian leader had "reaffirmed the one-China principle," something Malaysian analysts said isn't true. Malaysia has not abandoned its traditional position, but Anwar's rhetoric "has sometimes been more accommodating towards Beijing than necessary," Khoo Ying Hooi, associate professor of international relations at Universiti Malaya, told DW. "That can create the perception of a tilt even when Malaysia's wider strategic behavior remains more hedged and pragmatic," she added. Malaysia has less room to hedge The prime minister faces mounting political pressure after his Pakatan Harapan coalition suffered three consecutive setbacks in state elections. The defeats have intensified tensions within Anwar's broad governing alliance and speculation that he could call a snap general election. Yet beyond Anwar's rhetoric and domestic political calculations lies a more structural problem for Malaysia. Its longstanding strategy of hedging between the United States and China is becoming more difficult as Beijing's economic and military weight grows and Washington takes an increasingly transactional approach to foreign relations. "Malaysia is not abandoning its traditional balancing strategy, but the space for ambiguity is narrowing," said Hooi. Anwar is expected to visit China in late September, his first trip there in more than a year. He is reportedly due to attend the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou and hold talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang as Kuala Lumpur seeks to deepen economic ties with its largest trading partner. But closer relations with Beijing do not remove Malaysia's dependence on Western markets, investment and technology, or its own differences with China. Despite warm political ties, Kuala Lumpur continues to reject Chinese maritime claims in the South China Sea that overlap with waters Malaysia considers its own. In February, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan reiterated that Malaysia would not recognize Chinese claims that conflict with its maritime boundaries in the South China Sea, while Anwar has recently insisted that Malaysian oil and gas exploration will continue in the waters despite objections from Beijing. For Tan of the University of Nottingham, Malaysia's ability to continue balancing the two powers ultimately depends less on Anwar's rhetoric than on Malaysia remaining valuable to both. "China wants friendly neighbors to keep trading with, and America needs Malaysian factories, where a big share of the world's chips is tested and packaged," said Tan. "Neither gains from pushing Malaysia toward the other." Edited by: Ole Tangen Jr

item.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.28
Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014. Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday. Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions. Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded? The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023. Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine, and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead. "Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko. Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov, for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived. The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard. "The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement. Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo. "Russia can demand that the district court reassess the case," the Justice Ministry said. How did Russia respond? Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. "We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said. The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint. The Professor Molchanov, a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them. "The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website. He said that for the time being, "the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case. What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement? Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people. It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century. The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa, provided they met certain conditions. The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades. Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago. Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Nepal: Two pulled alive from tunnel nine days after floods
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.27
Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, nine days after catastrophic floods swept through the country's border region with China. Emergency teams are continuing efforts to reach hundreds more believed trapped inside similar tunnels. The men, identified as mechanical foreman Sanjay Shah and mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan, were freed from the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station's tunnel along the Trishuli River, according to a statement from the office of Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha. "As long as there is breath, there is hope!" Shrestha said in a statement. "Rescue operations are continuing in all the affected tunnels. Let everyone's efforts and prayers continue. We have not lost hope." What do we know about the rescue? Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, authorities said. Video and photos showed Maharjan, 45, pulled from a hole in the ground as bystanders cheered. Images showed him being placed on a stretcher, while Shah, 30, whose face was covered in mud, was carried out on a worker's back to a rescue tent, where army doctors fitted him with an oxygen mask and checked his vitals. An aide to the energy minister said Maharjan could not move his hands or legs, while Shah's injuries were not considered critical. Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Family members reacted with relief. Amir Maharjan, Kabir's brother, told the Associated Press, "I can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god," adding that the family was heading to the hospital to see him. What is happening at the hydropower project sites? These were the first successful rescues concerning the hydropower projects along the Trishuli River. Officials say as many as 900 workers remain missing across a number of project sites, with roughly 500 believed trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities. At the Trishuli 3A project specifically, the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal put the number of missing workers at 557, with about 115 believed trapped in the main tunnel. Nepal's communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials remained hopeful more survivors would be found: "We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people," he said. A team of experts coordinating through a WhatsApp group has been guiding rescue crews at the sites, becoming a key tool alongside helicopters and heavy machinery in the search effort. What is the scale of damage caused by the Nepal floods? Separately, Nepal's disaster authority estimated the floods caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.56 billion, €2.20 billion) in damage to property, housing and infrastructure, Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told Reuters. He said the first four months of early recovery — including rebuilding roads, setting up temporary shelters, and restoring water and power — would cost an estimated $52.6 million. "These are estimated amounts. We have calculated this in coordination with different concerned agencies and departments," Upreti said, noting a more detailed assessment would follow. He said Nepal would need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-affected areas, with at least 7,500 destroyed outright. The floods on August 26 were triggered by the collapse of a glacier upstream on the Trishuli River that sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through towns and villages near the Nepal-China border. At least 1,259 people have been killed in Nepal, according to the country's disaster management agency, with more than 5,000 still missing. China reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing on the Tibet side of the border as of late Wednesday. Edited by: Natalie Muller Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Germany, partners aim to finalize 'return hubs' by year end
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.18
Germany and other European Union countries are aiming to finalize so-called "return hubs," detention centers outside the bloc where they wish to send migrants whose asylum requests have been rejected, by the end of the year. The European Parliament in June approved tougher migration rules that paved the way for the creation of "return hubs." "We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year," which would then enable the establishment of so-called "return hubs," said German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt after a meeting with his counterparts from Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands in Copenhagen on Friday. He added that "technical discussions" were currently underway with countries outside the EU, but did not name such countries. What did the EU ministers say on 'return hubs?' The five EU countries whose ministers attended the Copenhagen meeting are seeking a deal with an undisclosed non-EU country to host the "return hubs." Uganda and Rwanda in particular are seen as possibilities —two autocratically ruled countries. "Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union," said Danish Migrations Minister Morten Bodskov. Both the Greek and Danish migration ministers said they wished for the "return hubs" to become operational by 2027. "We do not accept that foreigners staying illegally in Denmark should be rewarded because of our difficulties in returning them," Bodskov said in an earlier statement. The controversial scheme had already been briefly adopted by the United Kingdom under the former conservative government, but has since been scrapped after the social democratic Labour Party came to power. In Italy, the right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni reached a similar deal with Albania which currently faces legal challenges. Are EU 'return hubs' legal? The legality of the plans for the so-called "return hubs" remains unclear under EU law. A legal appraisal issued by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in April concluded that the controversial Italian deportation centers in Albania do not violate European law. EU law does not in principle prohibit member states from establishing such centers outside their own territory. However, it stipulates that deportees continue to receive legal counsel and linguistic support, and are able to maintain contact with their families and the relevant authorities. Andreas Grünewald, a migration expert with the German evangelical charity Brot für die Welt (Bread for the World), questioned the feasibility of the plans, calling them "practically difficult to implement and highly problematic in terms of human rights." He said ministers risked running into "political dead ends." Rights organizations criticize EU 'return hubs' The highly controversial plan has been met with wide rejection from rights groups, including children's charities and church organizations, who have criticized the plans for what they see as the "criminalization of migration." Marta Welander from the International Rescue Committee (IRC), a global humanitarian aid, relief and development NGO, said the plans risk "normalizing detainment in prison-like facilities" and warned that deportees may face "persecution, torture or worse" in their destination countries. Caritas, a Catholic charity operating in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Slovakia, said that migrants risked becoming trapped in a "legal grey area" if "arbitrarily and indefinitely detained" in the hubs. Florian Westphal, CEO of Save The Children Germany, warned of the risks faced in particular by children and young people. "The planned return centers in third countries are places of uncertainty and carry the risk of massive violations of children's rights," he said. "Transferring children to states with which they have no connection, and where they face the risk of deprivation of liberty and are cut off from key figures in their lives, cannot be in their best interests. Children deserve unconditional protection, no matter where they come from or where they live." Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.04
On Tuesday morning, unknown perpetrators attempted to attack the power supply near the coal-fired power plant at Jänschwalde in the eastern state of Brandenburg, partly succeeding in their objective. Then, later the same evening, a substation near Cologne suffered a disruption in what is believed to have been an act of sabotage. On Wednesday, an explosion occurred near the railway station in the Bavarian city of Augsburg, caused by a hand grenade, according to investigators. In the early hours of Thursday, several incendiary devices were thrown onto a construction site in Munich, close to a number of defense companies. Then, on Thursday evening, a suspicious object was discovered at a power substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Investigators say a claim of responsibility has since been received. While it remains entirely unclear who was behind the attacks in Jänschwalde, Cologne and Augsburg, investigators in Munich have arrested at least two suspects, reportedly Bulgarian nationals. Already 160 attacks on critical infrastructure this year What all these incidents have in common is that they appear to have targeted so-called critical infrastructure: energy facilities, the rail network, companies of strategic importance to national security and defense contractors. Taken together, these sites can hardly be protected in their entirety. According to media reports citing an internal document, the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) has recorded 160 potential acts of sabotage and more than 700 suspicious drone sightings so far this year. People in Berlin express concern over Russia Even if the exact circumstances of each incident remain unclear, their rapid succession has created a growing sense of constant threat among the public. To find out how people are reacting, DW spoke to residents on the streets of Berlin. One woman described her immediate reaction: "Fear. I was just talking about it with a colleague. It makes me feel very uneasy. I think about it a lot, and yet no one really talks about it. Maybe it's because people are afraid and would rather push it out of their minds?" One man added: "We first need to recognize that something is happening, that we are under attack. I have very close ties to Russia and very close Russian friends, and it is very, very painful to see what is happening." A freeze in German-Russian relations The fact that Russia is the first thing that comes to many people's minds when they hear about the recent wave of attacks is hardly surprising. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), both members of the governing alliance with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), appeared before the press. They announced that the German government is convinced Russian actors were behind the attempted drone attack on Halle/Leipzig Airport on August 4. The government responded by closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the lease on the Russian House in Berlin. Moscow, in turn, retaliated by shutting down the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. Relations between Germany and Russia are now at their lowest point in years. "We are no longer at peace, but neither are we at war," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) remarked last year. The reality is that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in the spring of 2022, Germany has been among Ukraine's strongest supporters, both financially and militarily. That holds true even though successive German governments, including the current one, have consistently maintained that the country is not itself a party to the war. Germany's support for Ukraine as a motive? Since then, the Bundeswehr, after years of continuous downsizing, has undergone rapid rearmament, driven in part by concerns that Russia could pose a threat even to central Europe. Neither at war nor at peace: Sönke Marahrens, a colonel in the German armed forces and a security expert at Kiel University, believes Germans would be well advised to prepare for this new form of confrontation, whoever may be responsible for it. He told DW: "Hybrid warfare and hybrid activities are, in my view, essentially the same thing because they rely on the same methods. Foreign states or organizations pursue their strategic interests without resorting to diplomacy. This can take the form of sabotage, disinformation or attacks on critical infrastructure." At the same time, the researcher stresses that it would be difficult to describe the situation as a state of war. Private firms urged to strengthen infrastructure security But it would be too simplistic to attribute every such incident immediately and unequivocally to Russia. Earlier this year, for example, an attack on a cable bridge in southwest Berlin caused a power outage that lasted several days. Hundreds of thousands of people were affected in freezing temperatures. In that case, which remains unsolved, suspicion has fallen on far-left extremists. A debate has long been underway in Germany over how best to prepare for such attacks in the future. This spring, the government passed legislation known as "KRITIS," aimed at strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure, although the law has yet to enter into force. Herbert Reul (CDU), the interior minister of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, noted in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF that critical facilities, including those operated by private companies, can already be monitored through video surveillance. Responsibility for securing the surrounding areas, however, lies with authorities such as the police. As Reul put it: "In Germany, we are sensitive when it comes to video surveillance and, more generally, to measures that affect civil liberties or data protection." Reul argued that companies themselves need to invest more in protecting their facilities. The German Police Union (DPolG) takes a similar view. Its chairman, Heiko Teggatz, said that safeguarding critical infrastructure is not primarily the responsibility of the police, but first and foremost of the operators themselves. "Those responsible for the security of their facilities must also invest in their protection," Teggatz said. What is lacking, he argued, is not technical capability but a consistent willingness to invest. This article was translated from German.

item.title: India news: Jaishankar offers help to end war in Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.96
What you need to know - India's foreign minister on tour of Poland and Ukraine - US Secretary of State has responded to a key meeting between Indian PM Narendra Modi and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian - A retired Air Marshal of the Indian Air Force has been tapped to be the first CEO of the controversy-mired Ram Temple in Ayodhya This blog is now closed. Here is a roundup of the latest developments from India on Thursday, September 3. Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. India wants tariff edge before signing US trade deal, says commerce minister India will announce the final details of its proposed Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) with the US only after Washington agrees to offer preferential tariff terms over India's competitors, Indian commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said on Thursday. "As soon as the US is able to give us the preferential rate in comparison to our competition, we will finalize the BTA and announce the final details," Indian news agencies quoted Goyal as saying. US President Donald Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi first announced negotiations for the US-India Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) in February 2025. But strained ties and global conflicts have delayed negotiations, with the talks only restoring momentum this year. In February, Washington and New Delhi released the framework for an interim trade agreement. Under the deal, India will "eliminate or reduce tariffs" on all US industrial products and a wide range of US food and agricultural goods. The US agreed to reduce Trump's tariffs from 25% to 18% and rescind the punitive extra 25% tariff imposed on India for its purchase of Russian oil. But negotiations on the final deal were deferred after the US Supreme Court struck down the Trump administration's sweeping tariffs. In June, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer visited New Delhi, where he met Goyal and reviewed core elements of the BTA. Goyal is now set to travel to the US later this month for the G20 Trade Ministerial in Milwaukee and engage in bilateral talks with Greer. India ready to help end Ukraine war, Jaishankar says during Kyiv visit India is ready to help end the war in Ukraine, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said as he arrived in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Thursday. "If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there," Jaishankar said as he addressed the media alongside Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. Sybiha welcomed Jaishankar for what he described as the "first-ever dedicated bilateral visit" of an Indian foreign minister to Ukraine. "India is a global power and we welcome Prime Minister Modi's call to move from an endless war towards an end to the war. Ukraine stands ready for diplomacy," Sybiha wrote on X, referring to comments the Indian leader made during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan earlier in the week. Jaishankar's trip to Ukraine comes more than a week after he attended the 27th session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation in Moscow with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov. The Indian foreign minister also met Putin during the Russia visit. Since the start of Russia's war in Ukraine, New Delhi has been under pressure from Kyiv's Western partners over its cooperation with Moscow, India's decades-long ally. "This historic moment takes place amid escalating Russian attacks against our cities, port infrastructure, and civil shipping. Our capital is constantly under attack and I appreciate my colleague's brave visit," Sybiha said as he talked about Jaishankar's Kyiv visit. The Ukrainian minister added that he and Jaishankar discussed the need to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, global food security, and bilateral cooperation. "From infrastructure and pharmaceutical sector to technological innovation and digitalisation, we are ready to realise our full potential," Sybiha said. Air Force veteran to be Ram Temple's first CEO A trust that runs India's grand Ram Temple in Ayodhya has roped in an Indian Air Force veteran to be the Hindu shrine's first chief executive officer (CEO) in a leadership shake-up following a donation embezzlement row, Indian media reported. Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, who retired from the Air Force in April 2026, was appointed CEO of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust on Wednesday. According to news agency ANI, more than 5,000 applicants were vying for the post. The temple in Uttar Pradesh was inaugurated in 2024 by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, fulfilling a key Hindu nationalist pledge. The temple site has been a controversial flashpoint because it was built on grounds where the 16th-century Babri Masjid, or Mosque of Babur, once stood. The mosque was demolished by Hindu mobs in 1992, triggering bloody riots that left nearly 2,000 people dead. Mishra's appointment comes after the Ram Temple became embroiled in controversy in recent months following allegations of theft involving donations and offerings worth millions of rupees. Mishra served as chief of the Indian Air Force's Western Command during the 2025 Indian military strikes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, which New Delhi said targeted "terrorist infrastructure" in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. "I also consider this the blessings of Lord Ram that after 43 years of service to the nation in the Air Force, He has given me the opportunity to serve Shri Ram Mandir (temple) and Shri Ram bhakt (devotees)," Mishra told news agency ANI. Opposition slams move The appointment has also drawn political criticism, particularly in the wake of the donation-related allegations surrounding the temple trust. The opposition Congress party has questioned Mishra's appointment. "Will appointing a new CEO or bringing in new people in the Trust bring back the donations by devotees? Has action been taken against the thieves?" Uttar Pradesh Congress chief Ajay Rai said in an interview with ANI. "Will the retired Air Marshal take action against these thieves and send them to jail? When will the action be taken and the stolen money be brought back?" he added. Congress leader Imran Masood told news agency PTI that the job was for "saints and seers." "Now, instead of saints and seers working inside the Ram Temple, a retired Air Marshal will be doing the work," he said. US Secretary of State Rubio reacts to Modi- Pezeshkian meeting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said he does not believe India and Iran are discussing a trade deal, two days after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modiheld a bilateral meeting with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the SCO in Bishkek. The Monday meeting between Modi and Pezeshkian was their first since the start of the Iran war. Rubio reacted to the leaders' meeting during an interview on "The Brian Kilmeade Show" on Fox News Radio on Wednesday. When asked by the host whether New Delhi and Tehran were pursuing some form of trade deal, Rubio said: "Well, I don't think there's a trade deal between India and Iran. Obviously, there are - countries all develop their own foreign policy, and many countries around the world talk to the Iranian regime." Later in the interview, the secretary of state issued a sanctions warning and reiterated US President Donald Trump's stance that no nation should help Iran evade sanctions. "No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon. And if countries decide to do that, then we're going to have to sanction them too," Rubio said. Foreign Minister S Jaishankar arrives in Poland, next stop Ukraine India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has reached the Polish capital of Warsaw as he kickstarts an official visit to Poland and Ukraine on Thursday. During the three-day tour, which runs until Saturday, Jaishankar is scheduled to meet Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha for bilateral consultations, the foreign ministry in New Delhi said in a statement. The ministry added that the visit is focused on "enhancing bilateral relations" and will also provide an opportunity to "exchange views on regional developments and issues of mutual interest." The foreign minister was greeted at the airport in Warsaw on Wednesday by India's ambassador to Poland, Neeta Bhushan. Jaishankar's trip to Poland comes amid speculation about a visit by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to India. Earlier in August, Poland's top envoy to India said that Tusk's visit, which would be his third to New Delhi, would send a strong signal for cooperation. There is yet to be formal confirmation of Tusk's India tour. The visit also reflects broader efforts by New Delhi to deepen engagement with Central and Eastern European partners. Following the Poland leg of his tour, Jaishankar will head to Ukraine. Jaishankar's Ukraine visit comes after key Modi-Putin meeting The Ukraine leg of Jaishankar's tour comes days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Monday. During the meeting, Modi urged an end to the war in Ukraine. Ahead of Jaishankar's arrival in Kyiv, Ukraine's First Deputy Head of the Office of the President, Sergiy Kyslytsya, said on Tuesday that he had met India's Ambassador to Ukraine, Anjani Kumar, to discuss Kyiv-New Delhi ties and India's role in efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine. Kyslytsya said he discussed with Kumar Modi's message to Putin in Bishkek, in which the Indian prime minister urged a "move from endless war to end of war" in Ukraine. "We look forward to continued dialogue with India and to translating this shared interest in peace into concrete steps," Kyslytsya added. Welcome to our coverage This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily roundup of the biggest headlines making a splash in India. India's Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar is embarking on a trip to Poland and Ukraine today, where he is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with his counterparts. Jaishankar's visit comes on the heels of a meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) earlier this week, where Modi urged close ally Putin to move from an "endless war" to "an end of war" in Ukraine. In more diplomatic news, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reacted to a meeting between Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Meanwhile, in domestic news, Ayodhya's Ram Temple will now have an Air Force veteran as its first chief executive officer following a donation theft controversy. We will cover that and more in this blog.

item.title: Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.85
Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging. More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost 4,000 are still missing. Buildings, bridges, roads and more than a dozen hydropower facilities have been destroyed, causing an estimated $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in damage to public and private infrastructure, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). Search and rescue operations for missing people remain underway, with families still hoping for their safe return. The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear, but experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters. A global responsibility? For Nepal, the disaster has raised a question that goes beyond rescue and reconstruction. It's about climate justice and who should bear the costs and responsibility for such environmental disasters when the Himalayan nation contributes only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces increasingly severe climate-related risks. Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said responding to the catastrophe is a "global responsibility." "As we work tirelessly to address the damage caused by this sudden and massive disaster, a deeper question has also emerged: How did this destruction happen to us?" Shah asked while addressing Parliament this week. "Mitigating and managing its impacts is regarded as a shared responsibility of the international community," he stressed. Kathmandu is planning to raise climate justice issues in the upcoming United Nations General Assembly session in New York, where Prime Minister Shah himself is likely to lead the Nepali delegation. "We will make our case about the impact of climate change and seek global support and moral obligation to tackle it," Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told DW. "We will also take the initiative of building a coalition of climate-vulnerable countries to raise our collective concerns." Highly vulnerable to climate impacts Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming. The country accounts for just 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions and emits about 0.5 tons of CO₂ per person each year, making it a "negligible contributor to climate change," according to the World Bank. But the landlocked Himalayan nation is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with flooding, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other environmental risks threatening lives and livelihoods. Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment. The country's government estimates that implementing adaptation priorities between 2025 and 2035 could require as much as $18 billion to $20 billion. And Kathmandu wants international climate finance to provide most of these funds. Nepal has spent years arguing in global climate forums that vulnerable mountain countries need greater support for adaptation and resilience. In December 2009, Nepal held a historic Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar, near Mount Everest base camp, at an altitude of 17,192 feet, to highlight the threats that climate change and glacial melting pose to Nepal and other mountainous nations. Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Nepali foreign minister, said the latest disaster meant "this is an opportune time for us to highlight glacier melting and climate justice issues in international climate forums." "Earlier, we were only advocating about climate impacts. Now, we are heavily suffering from it," she told DW. Paudyal believes Nepal is well positioned to lead an alliance of vulnerable countries, given its exposure to climate risk as well as its expertise and contribution to the climate justice effort. An opportunity for global climate action? Kathmandu has formally approached the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed "Loss and Damage Fund" for assistance over the latest floods. But the fund, set up by the UN in 2025 to aid the impacts of climate change, has not yet begun distributing its limited cash. The fund also relies on voluntary contributions and lacks legally binding commitments under current international climate agreements, leaving major emitters such as China, India and the US under no direct obligation to compensate for climate change impacts. Still, some observers and climate advocates believe Nepal can present a strong case for urgent global climate action. "Nepal can turn this tragedy into an opportunity for global climate action," Dinesh Paudel, professor of sustainable development at Appalachian State University in North Carolina, told DW. "For which, Nepal needs to build a consensus among national stakeholders and maneuver cautiously, considering geopolitical factors." According to him, Kathmandu can create an ethical movement for climate justice by highlighting the recent flood. This could then lead to creating an effective and legally binding mechanism to deal with climate impacts in the future. Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University and also UNESCO Chair on International Water Cooperation, shares a similar view. "Nepal should not be left to pay for a climate crisis it did little to create or for regional non-cooperation over which it has limited influence," he said. "This is not a question of charity. It is fundamentally a question of climate justice and a fair distribution of responsibility." Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.82
What you need to know - India has carried out a successful launch of its EOS-05 Earth observation satellite - India ace Smriti Mandhana is now the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket - Air India begins voluntary testing for all its pilots after probe agency finds drug test of a captain "non-negative" in August air incident This blow is now closed. Read below for a roundup of the latest developments from India on Friday, September 4. Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. WATCH — How AI uses up water AI is driving a boom in data centers and a surge in water use. In India, where water is already scarce in many places, campaigners say that cost must be taken into account when new infrastructure is planned. Find out more in this report: Air India probe flags triple hydraulic loss, pilot drug test An Air India plane which experienced a sudden drop in altitude while flying from Phuket to New Delhi last month suffered a temporary loss of hydraulic systems, Indian investigators have said. The plane's pilot also returned a "non-negative" result in a confirmatory test for psychoactive substances, India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) said in a preliminary report on Friday. The body is probing the incident involving the Air India A320 flight, which plummeted 300 feet (91 meters) on August 4 while cruising over the Indian state of Odisha, before recovering and landing safely in Delhi. A total of 20 passengers and four crew members were injured. Following the incident, Indian media reports said that the primary captain of the flight tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test. On Friday, the AAIB, updated the event, which was earlier classified as a "serious incident" to an "accident." What did the probe agency say? The AAIB said that the flight-control system detected the loss of all three of the aircraft's hydraulic systems for several seconds. "The aircraft encountered altitude upset," it said in the report, adding that the plane gained 372 feet initially and fell by 292 feet. A two-second stall warning came after the hydraulic failure, disengaging the autopilot and setting off a continuous cockpit alarm, the report said. The stall warning came when the seatbelt signs were off and the rapid pitch up and down threw those on board against the overhead bins, leading to the injuries, the report elaborated. "Subsequently, the aircraft operation returned to its normal operating condition," the agency's report said. The report went on to add that the pilot-in-command returned a "non-negative" test for psychoactive substances. "The confirmation of use of psychoactive substance is a serious concern," it said without identifying the substance. What has Air India said? Following Friday's report, Air India released a statement saying that it had started voluntary testing of "100% of its pilots" after the incident as "a further step to reinforce its safety-first approach." "We acknowledge the release of the preliminary report by the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) and continue to extend our full cooperation to the investigation, including providing access to all relevant operational, maintenance and technical records," the Indian flag carrier said. Smriti Mandhana becomes women's international cricket's leading run-scorer India vice-captain Smriti Mandhana has smashed records to become the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket. Mandhana's total runs now stand at 10,880 as she surpassed former India captain Mithali Raj'srally of 10,868 runs on the international scoreboard. Madhana achieved the feat as she knocked out a century during team India's win against Hong Kong in the Women's Asia Cup on Thursday. The ton, which was Madhana's 18th international hundred, also marked the most centuries by a player in women's international cricket. "I didn't know all of this happened," the 30-year-old left hander said after scripting history. "But I love batting and am happy to contribute. There are days when you hit balls from the stumps. There are days when you edge one. It's extremely unpredictable." Former record-holder Raj has congratulated Mandhana. "To see you go past my record and become the highest run-scorer in international cricket is a moment I'm genuinely proud of. Here's to many more runs and milestones. Keep going!" she wrote on X. India launches key Earth observation satellite The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) on Friday successfully deployed the country's first ever imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit. A Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) — carrying the EOS-05 Earth observation satellite — lifted off from ISRO's primary spaceport, the Satish Dhawan Space Center in Sriharikota, at 2:55 a.m. local time (2125 UTC). The Indian space agency shared visuals of the countdown for the launch which ended with the GSLV-F17 firing up and lifting off, lighting up the dark early morning skies in its wake. About 18 minutes later, ISRO announced that the satellite was successfully placed in the intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit. ISRO proclaimed "Mission Success!" in a post on X. ISRO's first success in 2026 The launch marked the 19th flight of India's GSLV. It was also ISRO's first success this year after a mission setback in January saw a Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle rocket failing to place 16 satellites in the intended orbit The EOS-05 — with a payload of over 2,300 kilograms — is the country's heaviest ever satellite to be carried by a GSLV. The satellite — dubbed as India's "eye in the sky" — will operate from an altitude of roughly 36,000 kilometers above Earth, which is higher than typical low-Earth-orbit observation satellites The satellite will match the home planet's rotational speed. Its expected mandate is to bolster India's ability to obtain frequent imagery of large areas for applications including Earth observation and monitoring. "The health of the satellite is perfectly alright," ISRO Chairman V Narayanan said after the launch. PM Modi lauds India's growing space capabilities On Friday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the satellite's launch as "yet another outstanding achievement" by the Indian space agency and "a proud moment" for the country. "The successful launch of GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05, India's first-ever imaging satellite from Geosynchronous orbit is a reflection of the excellence, innovation and growing capabilities that define India's space sector," he said on X. Welcome to our coverage This is Dharvi from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our Friday edition of the India news blog, where we give you a round up of all the biggest headlines that have got people talking across the country. In the early hours of the morning, India successfully launched its first ever imaging satellite in the geosynchronous orbit, etching a milestone in the country's space program. Another feat was notched — this time in the world of cricket — as India batter Smriti Mandhana became the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket. Meanwhile, in diplomatic news, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar has wrapped up a visit to Kyiv that came amid India's renewed push for peace in Russia's war in Ukraine. Follow along as we bring you more.

item.title: 2026 Beethoven Festival evokes a sense of home
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.71
Four trumpeters will be scattered throughout the concert hall, accompanied by organ music, promising a magnificent auditory experience in Bonn's newly renovated Beethovenhalle on Friday evening. The piece "A Call to the Heavens" was composed by Stefan Behrisch specifically for the opening of this year's Beethovenfest. Additionally, the London Symphony Orchestra, led by principal conductor Sir Antonio Pappano, will perform Ludwig van Beethoven's "Die Weihe des Hauses" ("The Consecration of the House") as well as Bruckner's Symphony No. 9 at the opening concert. For nine years, Bonn's Beethovenhalle, a designated historic landmark, was unavailable for the festival. But now, as Philipp Seliger, spokesperson for the Beethoven Festival explained, "we have a large concert hall again with its excellent original acoustics. "We can once again invite major renowned orchestras because we have the appropriate stage and infrastructure," Seliger added. This also prompted Hungarian star pianist, Andras Schiff, to perform at the festival this year. Musical home for everyone The new hall isn't only intended to make stars and major orchestras feel at home — the audience and local musicians ought to feel that way too. Indeed, for local musicians, there is a specially designed Festival Salon where local communities and bands can create their own programs. And anyone can come by and participate in the "Meet your band" project, which is an accessible, free program for people who otherwise wouldn't visit a classical concert hall. The Beethovenfest also reaches out to people in neighborhoods across the city, right where they live. For over a year, as a part of this effort, Juri de Marco and the "Community Choir" have been encouraging people to sing and improvise, regardless of whether they can read music. "For me, home is more a feeling than it is a place. It's where you can rely on a genuine social network, where people notice when you are absent," said festival director Steven Walter, who himself has lived in various places around the world. "Everywhere I go, my sense of well-being depends on my social connections." Beethoven reinterpreted Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1850, and died in Vienna in 1827. Next year marks the 200th anniversary of his death, and to celebrate, pianist Kit Armstrong with conductor Jan Caeyers, along with his orchestra "Le Concert Olympique," are launching "Beethoven 27," a major Beethoven cycle. In nine concerts, they will present entirely new interpretations of Beethoven's nine symphonies, as well as his sonatas and piano concertos. The first three concerts will be presented at this year's Beethovenfest. Caeyers has devoted himself to Beethoven, not only as a conductor but also as a musicologist. He is the author of the acclaimed biography "Beethoven: A Life," but said he is far from finished discovering the composer. "Every time I immerse myself in Beethoven, new and unexpected doors open. That's what keeps me fascinated," Caeyers told DW. Armstrong feels the same way. "There isn't just one Beethoven," he said. "There are countless images and perspectives of Beethoven, including many that emerged long after his death. Those perspectives should also inform the way we interpret his music today." Spotlight on Georgia Artists at this year's Beethovenfest will introduce music from their homelands. Among them is Palestinian-Syrian pianist Aeham Ahmad, who gained global renown for playing the piano amid the rubble of the Syrian civil war. Violinist Lisa Batiashvili, who was born in Georgia, is this year's artist in residence at the Beethovenfest. Performing with the Dresden Philharmonic, she will present works from her homeland as part of the program "City Lights" — a personal tribute to Georgia, which the festival is spotlighting this year. As part of the festival's long-running "Campus" youth exchange program, young musicians from Georgia and Germany will collaborate, with Beethoven's music performed alongside works by leading Georgian composers. The entire ensemble will also perform Heinrich Schütz's five-part motet "Verleih uns Frieden gnädiglich" ("Grant Us Gracious Peace"). Musicians from Germany's National Youth Orchestra and the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra held their joint rehearsal residency in June, developing their own artistic vision and program for Beethovenfest. The project also explores how young artists see themselves in a country facing political turmoil, where the path toward Europe has repeatedly shifted course. Seventeen-year-old composer and pianist Tsotne Zedginidze, regarded as one of Georgia's most extraordinary young musical talents, was commissioned to write the Campus project's new work. Beyond classical music Crossovers, musical fusion and new ideas for the future of music remain central to this year's Beethovenfest. Two musical worlds will come together with Senegalese kora player Momi Maiga joining the string orchestra "Ensemble Resonanz" to improvise on Beethoven's music. American composer Brittany J. Green will experiment with artificial intelligence and visual effects in her work "gLitchED dreams//invisible BEINGS." Performed with the music collective "Alarm Will Sound," the piece creates a sonic landscape inspired by the digital age. "We're looking for the Beethovens of our time," said spokesperson Seliger, "including people who aren't necessarily composers of classical music." Beethovenfest runs from Sept. 3 through Oct. 3, 2026. DW is a media partner and co-shareholder of the festival. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs by end of decade
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.31
German automobile giant Volkswagen announced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry. The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed. "It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audi and Porsche. The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009. Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not being honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally. 'The motor of the entire region' What's more, Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed. Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country. "If this plant really were shut down, you could put a big black spot on the map," one long-term employee in Zwickau, Saxony, told the AFP news agency. "The plant and the jobs outside it, our suppliers, they're the motor of the entire region." Caught between US tariffs, Chinese competition and a sluggish growth in demand for electric vehicles, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble. Company reforms to drive profitability However, CEO Oliver Blume insisted that the decision to cut 100,000 jobs sent "a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group." Volkswagen did not give details as to the timing of the cuts and how they would be distributed across the different regions where it has plants and offices, but the company said its focus will turn to North America and that it is looking to expand exports to the Global South. The plan also includes a three-digit-billion sum investment over the coming years as VW looks to improve technologically through research and development and become more competitive. Among the moves is a structural change that should bring about faster decision-making and a cut to the number of businesses and holdings it owns by about one-third. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
