item.title: The 10 most streamed songs of all time on Spotify — and the stories behind them
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.63
The 10 most streamed songs of all time on Spotify — and the stories behind them The most streamed songs on Spotify of all time show how pop's biggest hits earned their staying power, from The Weeknd to Ed Sheeran A song needs about four billion plays to make Spotify $SPOT's all-time top 10 now, a number that would have sounded like a typo a decade ago. The most streamed songs on Spotify tell two different stories depending on how they got there. Some, like a synth-heavy Weeknd single or a Harry Styles lead single, hit that scale through pure, immediate saturation: radio play, playlists, and a release cycle built for maximum reach. Others got there the slow way, picking up more streams years after release than they did in their first month, revived by a TikTok trend, a Spider-Man movie, or a wedding season that never really ends. That mix is what makes this list useful beyond trivia. It is a rough map of how listening habits have actually changed since Spotify became the default way people hear new music. A 2012 alt-rock song about a fight in a car can now out-stream most of what topped the actual Billboard charts that year, because a platform most listeners had never opened yet turned it into an anthem for a very online generation eight years later. A ballad written by a Scottish singer nobody outside the U.K. had heard of can out-stream stadium tours, because grief and heartbreak translate across every market Spotify operates in without needing a single radio play. Streaming numbers shift daily, so any snapshot of this list is exactly that: a snapshot. The ranking below reflects Spotify's own count of all-time streams as of September 2026, and every song on it has already crossed four billion plays, a threshold that only a handful of releases per year manage to reach at all. What follows is not just the count next to each title. It is the writing session that almost got scrapped, the sample clearance that turned into a lawsuit, the movie placement nobody predicted would outlast the movie's own soundtrack sales. Those details explain why these 10 songs, out of the tens of millions available on the platform, are the ones that never stopped getting played. Blinding Lights by The Weeknd is Spotify's most streamed song ever Blinding Lights has been streamed more than 5.5 billion times on Spotify $SPOT, more than any other song on the platform. The Weeknd, born Abel Tesfaye, released it in November 2019 as the second single from his album After Hours, and it has not relinquished the top spot on Spotify's all-time chart since. Tesfaye wrote the song with Max Martin, one of pop's most successful songwriter-producers, and Oscar Holter, with additional production from Jason Quenneville and Ahmad Balshe. The track pulls from 1980s synth-pop, layering a driving bassline under Tesfaye's falsetto in a way that made it as recognizable on classic-rock-adjacent radio as on pop stations built for younger listeners. That crossover appeal is part of why it kept climbing charts built for entirely different audiences at once. Its Billboard Hot 100 run set records that will be difficult for any future song to break. Blinding Lights spent 90 weeks total on the chart, 57 of them inside the top 10 and 43 inside the top five, both all-time records. In 2021, Billboard named it the number one song in the Hot 100's entire history to that point, ahead of decades-old staples like Chubby Checker's The Twist. Part of the song's staying power on Spotify specifically comes from timing. It hit its commercial peak in the spring of 2020, just as much of the world went into pandemic lockdown and streaming became, for many people, the primary way they experienced new music at all. The song's retro, neon-lit music video and its steady use across workout and driving playlists have kept it circulating years after its initial chart run ended. The Weeknd has had other massive Spotify hits, including Starboy and The Hills, but none has come close to matching Blinding Lights' pace. Every song on this list has needed years to accumulate its stream count. Blinding Lights reached the billion-stream mark faster than nearly any song before it and has continued adding tens of millions of streams a month, six years after its release, a pace that keeps widening its lead over Shape of You in second place. Shape of You made Ed Sheeran give away songwriting credit Shape of You sits at number two on Spotify $SPOT's all-time list with more than 5 billion streams, trailing only Blinding Lights. Ed Sheeran released it in January 2017 as the lead single from his third album, ÷, pronounced Divide, and it became one of the biggest-selling songs of that year worldwide. Sheeran wrote the track with Steve Mac and Snow Patrol's Johnny McDaid, and he has said the song was not originally written for himself. He told BBC Radio 1 that the trio started writing it with Rihanna in mind, only switching the vocal to Sheeran partway through the session once the lyrics felt too specific to his own life to hand off. The song's melody drew comparisons to TLC's 1999 hit No Scrubs almost immediately after release, and Sheeran's team added No Scrubs writers Kandi Burruss, Tameka Cottle, and Kevin Briggs as co-writers on Shape of You rather than contest the claim. That decision followed a pattern for Sheeran, who had already faced separate copyright disputes over his earlier songs Photograph and Thinking Out Loud. A second copyright case reached the U.K. High Court in 2022, when musician Sami Chokri argued the song's central Oh, I hook was lifted from his own 2015 track Oh Why. After an 11-day trial, a judge ruled Sheeran had neither deliberately nor unconsciously copied Chokri's song, closing one of the most closely watched music copyright cases of the decade. Shape of You also spent 16 weeks atop Canada's national singles chart, a record that stood until Lil Nas X $TWTR's Old Town Road broke it two years later, and it reached number one in the U.K., the U.S., and across most of Europe and Australia. Its Caribbean-inflected production, built around a marimba riff, helped push tropical house textures further into mainstream pop long after the genre's initial wave had faded from radio. Sweater Weather by The Neighbourhood found new life on TikTok Sweater Weather has been streamed nearly 4.9 billion times on Spotify $SPOT, making it the third most streamed song in the platform's history, and almost none of that came in the year it was released. The Neighbourhood put the song out in March 2012 as the fourth track from their debut EP, I'm Sorry, and it later appeared on their 2013 album I Love You. Frontman Jesse Rutherford has said the song grew out of tension inside the band rather than a moment of inspiration. According to the group, the track took shape after members got into a heated argument during a car ride back from the studio, and that friction shaped both the song's mood and its writing session. On release, it performed respectably but unremarkably, peaking at number 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 in December 2013. The real turning point came seven years later. In mid-2020, TikTok users began using Sweater Weather as a kind of code, pairing the song with clips announcing their sexuality to friends and family, drawing on the lyric one love, two mouths, one love, one house. The trend turned the song into an anthem within LGBTQ+ communities on the app and sent its streaming numbers soaring; it gained more than 5 million on-demand streams in a single month that November, a career high at the time. That resurgence pushed Sweater Weather onto the Billboard Global 200 more than eight years after its original release, a chart debut most songs never get even once. Its official music video later crossed 1 billion views on YouTube, placing The Neighbourhood alongside a small group of artists to reach that milestone with a single clip. The band's original independent video was pulled after they signed to Columbia Records, meaning most of that YouTube audience has only ever seen the later, re-released version. Few songs demonstrate as clearly how a streaming platform can hand an older, mid-charting single a second life larger than its first. Starboy marked The Weeknd killing off his old persona on camera Starboy has racked up more than 4.7 billion streams on Spotify $SPOT, and its music video may be the most literal reinvention story in modern pop. The Weeknd released the song in September 2016 as the title track and lead single from his third studio album, featuring French electronic duo Daft Punk, and it became his third number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and Daft Punk's only chart-topper as credited artists. Where earlier Weeknd hits leaned entirely on his own vocals and songwriting team, Starboy paired his voice with Daft Punk's production, giving the track a colder, more mechanical low end than his previous album, Beauty Behind the Madness. The shift in sound matched a visible shift in image: Tesfaye had worn the same signature long, teased hairstyle throughout his early career, and Starboy's rollout was built around cutting it off. Directed by longtime collaborator Grant Singer, the music video opens with a masked figure suffocating a version of Tesfaye still wearing his old hair, then reveals the killer as a new version of Tesfaye with the short haircut that appeared on the Starboy album cover. The new persona goes on to smash trophies, platinum plaques, and photographs from Tesfaye's earlier career using a glowing cross, then drives off in a sports car with a black panther in the passenger seat. Critics and fans read the video as a metaphor for reinvention: Tesfaye was ending the version of himself that broke through with mixtapes like House of Balloons and signaling a more polished, pop-facing chapter. The strategy extended well beyond the singles chart. Starboy's parent album debuted at number one in multiple countries, and the title track's blend of Daft Punk's robotic disco and Tesfaye's R&B falsetto helped normalize electronic-pop crossovers that other major pop acts leaned into over the following several years. As It Was captures Harry Styles' pandemic isolation As It Was has been streamed more than 4.6 billion times on Spotify $SPOT, making it Harry Styles' most streamed song by a wide margin. Released in March 2022 as the lead single from his third album, Harry's House, the synth-pop track opens with a recording of Styles' goddaughter, Ruby Winston, saying, Come on, Harry, we want to say goodnight to you. Styles wrote the song with longtime collaborators Kid Harpoon, whose real name is Tom Hull, and Tyler Johnson, recording much of Harry's House in a home studio set up inside Sony $SONY Music Group chief executive Rob Stringer's house in Henley-on-Thames, England. Harry's House itself opened at number one on the Billboard 200 the week of its release in May 2022, giving Styles his second consecutive album to debut on top of that chart after 2019's Fine Line. In interviews, Styles described the song as being about metamorphosis and change rather than any single relationship, and pointed to his own experience of isolation during pandemic lockdowns as a source for its lyrics. The song's second verse, which imagines a phone call in which someone worries Styles is not doing well alone, reflects the nightly calls he had with his goddaughter during lockdown, the same calls that produced the opening voice clip. Musically, the track pairs an upbeat, 1980s-influenced tempo with lyrics about loneliness and disconnection, a contrast Styles has said was deliberate. As It Was earned Styles nominations for record of the year and song of the year at the 2023 Grammy Awards, though it won neither award; its parent album, Harry's House, won album of the year that same night, beating out heavily favored records from Beyoncé and Adele. On the Billboard Hot 100, the song spent 15 weeks at number one, the most of any song by a British artist in the chart's history, and it debuted directly at number one in April 2022, a feat only a small number of songs have managed. One Dance introduced Afrobeats sounds to Spotify's global audience One Dance has been streamed more than 4.4 billion times on Spotify $SPOT and once held the title of the most streamed song in the platform's history outright. Drake released it in April 2016 as a single from his fourth album, Views, featuring Nigerian singer Wizkid and British singer Kyla, and it topped the singles charts in 15 countries, including the U.S., the U.K., and Canada. The song's foundation is a sample of Kyla's 2008 U.K. funky track Do You Mind, specifically the Crazy Cousinz remix, whose vocal and keyboard stabs anchor most of One Dance's melody. Kyla, whose own version had peaked at only number 48 on the U.K. Singles Chart eight years earlier, received a songwriting credit and a career revival once One Dance became a global hit, going on to perform at U.K. festivals including Wireless that same summer. Drake and Wizkid had already worked together before One Dance, teaming up on a 2015 remix of Wizkid's song Ojuelegba. That earlier collaboration set up One Dance as a more fully formed fusion of dancehall and Afrobeats, produced by Nineteen85 and Noah 40 Shebib alongside Wizkid himself. The result helped push Afrobeats, a genre built mostly in Lagos and London, into mainstream Western pop playlists years before artists like Burna Boy and Rema became global stars in their own right. On October 17, 2016, One Dance became the most streamed song in Spotify's history at that point, surpassing Major Lazer's Lean On, which had held the record for the previous 11 months. It has since been passed by newer entries including Shape of You and Blinding Lights, but it remains the highest-streamed song built primarily around a sampled vocal rather than an original topline, and one of the clearest commercial proof points for Afrobeats' crossover potential in the mid-2010s. Sunflower became the emotional anchor of Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse Sunflower has surpassed 4.4 billion streams on Spotify $SPOT, making it one of the best-performing movie soundtrack songs in streaming history. Post Malone and Swae Lee released it in October 2018 as the lead single from the soundtrack to Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, the animated film centered on teenage hero Miles Morales, before the song was later added to Post Malone's own album, Hollywood's Bleeding. Malone first confirmed his involvement with the film on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon in early October 2018, revealing he had written the song himself before Swae Lee, of the duo Rae Sremmurd, joined the recording. The two had already collaborated once before, on the track Spoil My Night from Malone's second album, Beerbongs and Bentleys, and Sunflower marked their second pairing within the same year. Swae Lee has described the song's placement in the film as one of his favorite creative moments, explaining that Miles Morales's character uses the song within the story to calm himself down during a stressful moment, a use he compared to the way his own music has functioned for listeners. The lyric video, built from the film's comic-book-style animation and lettering, later crossed 2 billion views on YouTube on its own, separate from the song's official music video. An official remix released in February 2019 added Latin singers Nicky Jam and Prince Royce, extending the song's reach into Spanish-language radio markets months after its initial release. Sunflower's lyrics describe a strained relationship in which both singers keep leaving and returning, using the sunflower itself as a symbol of loyalty and resilience under neglect. Written by Malone, Swae Lee, and producers Carter Lang and Louis Bell along with Billy Walsh and Carl Rosen, the song's warm, mid-tempo production stood apart from the darker trap-influenced sound Malone was known for at the time, helping it cross over to pop and adult contemporary radio formats that his earlier singles rarely reached. Someone You Loved nearly got scrapped by Lewis Capaldi Someone You Loved has been streamed more than 4.4 billion times on Spotify $SPOT, making it the biggest song of Scottish singer Lewis Capaldi's career by a wide margin. Released in November 2018 from his debut album, Divinely Uninspired to a Hellish Extent, the piano ballad topped the U.K. Singles Chart for seven consecutive weeks in 2019 and later reached number one in the U.S. after a slow climb up the Billboard Hot 100. Capaldi has said he almost abandoned the song entirely. He worked on it with the production and writing team TMS, made up of Thomas Barnes, Peter Kelleher, and Benjamin Kohn, along with co-writer Sam Romans, and the group spent close to six months on it. Capaldi told interviewers he kept scrapping his own drafts because he felt he had already written the same breakup song too many times before, until TMS pushed him to write about loss more broadly instead of one specific relationship. That shift is what gives the song its double meaning. Capaldi has confirmed the lyrics were written deliberately to work for someone mourning a breakup or someone mourning a death, without specifying which one he intended. Two official music videos reflect that ambiguity: one is a straightforward story about heartbreak, and the other features Capaldi's cousin, actor Peter Capaldi, in a narrative about organ donation, reframing the song's sense of loss around mortality rather than romance. Someone You Loved won song of the year at the 2020 Brit Awards, beating out bigger commercial hits from more established artists that year. Its stripped-down arrangement, built around a single piano chord loop with almost no percussion, left Capaldi's voice fully exposed on the recording, a production choice that made the song stand out on streaming platforms crowded with more heavily produced pop ballads at the time. Perfect turned into Ed Sheeran and Beyoncé's wedding duet Perfect has been streamed more than 4 billion times on Spotify $SPOT and has become one of the most requested songs at weddings worldwide. Ed Sheeran wrote it about his now-wife, Cherry Seaborn, and included it on his 2017 album, ÷, though it was released as a single later that September, well after the album's initial run of hits had already peaked. Sheeran has said the song's most personal line, about standing barefoot on the grass listening to their favorite song, came from a specific night in Ibiza, when the couple danced on a lawn to Future's song March Madness with no shoes on. He wrote and produced the track largely on his own, with Will Hicks handling additional production, giving Perfect a simpler, more stripped-down sound than the Caribbean-influenced Shape of You released earlier that same year. The solo version had already peaked at number four in the U.K. months earlier, a strong showing that set up the much bigger chart run once the duet arrived. The song's commercial peak arrived only after Sheeran released a duet version featuring Beyoncé in December 2017. Sheeran has said Perfect was reportedly Beyoncé's favorite track on ÷, which led him to email her directly about a collaboration, not expecting a yes. Beyoncé recorded her verse in a single take, and the resulting Perfect Duet pushed the song to number one on the Billboard Hot 100, a peak the solo version alone had not reached. A separate version, Perfect Symphony, released the same month, paired Sheeran with Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli, extending the song's reach into a completely different audience. Sheeran has spoken about writing love songs meant to outlast typical chart cycles, telling interviewers he would rather have people tell him a song was their wedding song for years to come than win an Album of the Year Grammy, and Perfect's slow, steady climb toward 4 billion Spotify streams has borne that preference out. Stay set a Billboard record for The Kid LAROI and Justin Bieber Stay has surpassed 4 billion streams on Spotify $SPOT and set an outright Billboard chart record for how long a single song can dominate the top of the Hot 100. The Kid LAROI, an Australian rapper born Charlton Howard, released the track with Justin Bieber in July 2021 as the lead single from his mixtape F*ck Love 3: Over You, and it went on to spend seven weeks at number one. The song began as an impromptu writing session at producer Blake Slatkin's house, where LAROI worked alongside Slatkin, Omer Fedi, Cashmere Cat, and rapper-producer Haan. LAROI has since clarified in interviews that he wrote nearly every lyric in the song himself, with the exception of Bieber's verse, pushing back on years of assumptions that producer Charlie Puth, who also worked on the track, had written a larger share of it. LAROI initially considered giving the unfinished song to Bieber for one of his own projects instead of releasing it himself. According to LAROI, Bieber refused outright, telling him the song was too strong to give away and that he needed to release it under his own name. Bieber later joined the recording with a verse addressed to his wife, Hailey, referencing his own past struggles with trust in the relationship. The music video, directed by Colin Tilley, places LAROI and Bieber inside a frozen, snow-covered world, matching the song's tone of two people stuck reliving the same argument. Beyond its seven weeks at number one, Stay set the record for the most weeks any song has spent in the Hot 100's top two positions, logging 20 weeks there across its chart run, a mark that included 13 additional weeks stuck at number two. The song also helped push LAROI's mixtape to number one on the Billboard 200 more than a year after its original release, an unusually long gap for an album to reach its commercial peak.

item.title: The Netherlands Will Never Be Rid of Louisiana Crawfish
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 4.24
Confronted with a seasoned, boiled, arguably delicious crayfish, some of the people of the Netherlands are not sure exactly what to do. “Do you suck the head out?” I heard from the table next to me earlier this summer, at Two Chefs, a restaurant in Amsterdam that hosts a monthly crayfish boil.
Yes is the answer: The best way to eat a crayfish is to shell the tail, then slurp the flavored juices out of the head, and pick out the remaining meat with your hands. This strategy might not be an immediate transatlantic hit. At the boil, one 29-year-old from Maastricht likened the meal to shrimp but with more work. Two twins told me that the crayfish would need to look a little more chic on the plate to appeal to the Dutch public. But, given the ever-growing population of crayfish in the Netherlands, coming around to eating more of them could benefit the country. Because if Dutch consumers aren’t sure how they feel about crayfish, crayfish inarguably love the Netherlands. They have invaded the country’s waterways so thoroughly that they have become a real problem, and dealing with them will mean persuading more creatures—including Dutch people—to eat more crayfish. The crayfish invasion started decades ago, but in recent years, the red swamp crayfish (also known as the Louisiana crawfish) has become a particular pest, Pim Lemmers, an ecologist at Radboud University who has dedicated his career to researching crayfish, told me. In the 1980s, it was brought to the Netherlands as food, and people naively released the animals into the environment. The waterways in the Netherlands are very interconnected and became a “crayfish highway” of sorts, Ivo Roessink, an aquatic ecotoxicologist at Wageningen University & Research, told me. But crayfish can walk and breathe on land, too, and have been spotted in parks, along bike lanes, and at Schiphol airport, where the birds use the runway to crush them. And they can dig—burrows up to three feet long that can collapse the edges of fields into the water and that some people fear could damage the country’s extensive system of dams, dikes, and canals. Scientists emphasize that the risk to dams and dikes is low; from their point of view, the bigger risk is to other creatures that live in the water. Crayfish are omnivorous: “They totally destroy underwater vegetation,” Roessink said. They also eat detritus, amphibian and insect larvae, snails and other invertebrates, small fish, and one another—a sight I witnessed for myself. But crayfish cannibalism will not end the invasion; in fact, although the Netherlands’ central government is working on a program for crayfish management, getting rid of the species will likely be impossible. “I know of one example where they effectively eradicated crayfish, and that was in the U.S.,” Roessink said. “There was an infected pond, and they turned it into a parking lot.” (Resorting to this solution in the Netherlands would require paving over the entire country.) Research in the Netherlands and elsewhere has shown that even extensive trapping won’t necessarily eliminate crayfish. The most anyone can hope for is fewer of them. Some water boards of the Netherlands are trying to persuade all sorts of creatures to eat more crayfish, including herons, eels, and European catfish, which are themselves something of an invasive threat. And, in theory, one of the crayfish’s most effective predators could be Dutch people. Stefan van Ekris and Maarten van der Sanden, who are both managing directors at CrawFish Farm Holland, are trying their best to make it happen. This July, I joined them as they put on waders and immersed themselves in irrigation ditches to set and check their crayfish nets in the Groene Hart, or “Green Heart,” of the Netherlands, the thinly populated pastures and peatlands among some of the country’s largest cities. They get paid per kilogram caught—the expedition I joined yielded about 150 kilograms, or 330 pounds, of live crayfish—but this is really a passion project for them. CrawFish Farm Holland is approved to sell live and prepared catch directly to restaurants and other wholesalers, and hopes to sell its crayfish in supermarkets in the next two years. “We’re not cultivating them,” Van der Sanden told me. “We’re fighting them and eating them.” In America, Van der Sanden pointed out, Louisiana was able to quickly ramp up crayfish production and demand in the 1980s. But the scientists I spoke with were skeptical of this strategy. “You will never eat yourself out of this crisis,” Roessink said. And if people like crayfish too much, Lemmers said, they might start cultivating crayfish in their backyard or trapping them without oversight, which could promote further spread. Even if more Dutch people come around to the pleasures of a messy boil, the crayfish still could come out ahead. The image originally accompanying this article did not show a red swamp crayfish. That image has been replaced.

item.title: Creating the Perfect Female Monster
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 4.15
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts The breakout crime drama Furious opens with a scene that’s hard to watch: Catherine, a serial killer played by Lola Petticrew, is keeping a man prisoner in a row house and taunting him as he dies: “I don’t like the sounds you’re making.” The show’s creator, Liz Meriwether, is announcing right away that you will be spending time with a monster, and the discomfort amps up from there. As the show progresses, we learn that Catherine has been trafficked, and the men she is killing were involved in her abuse. In an era when “Epstein Island” exists, Catherine represents a specific kind of psychopathic serial killer. She is, as the title suggests, one of the Furies exacting revenge in a world that hasn’t managed to execute justice for her the legal way. Meriwether says she did not set out to make a statement on the state of female rage or American justice, or even a commentary on Epstein, yet the show may have hit a nerve because those issues are so alive right now. Nine years ago, women’s anger fueled the MeToo movement, and it seemed as if the way society confronts sexual harassment and abuse was on the brink of transformation. “Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been,” the Atlantic staff writer Sophie Gilbert says. “And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb.” In this episode, Meriwether talks about the complications of humanizing a serial killer and how the project of creating complicated women characters has evolved in her decade of writing for television. And Gilbert talks about what it means that more women creators are owning the stories told about women. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: A female monster is a rare but recurring creature. She often emerges at moments in history when women in society are collectively angry at the powers that be but unable to express it. Maybe they’re too defeated or maybe numb, so the monster gets revenge for them. I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic. Right now, there is a particularly interesting monster out there taking revenge on a fictional Jeffrey Epstein. It’s playing out on the Hulu show Furious—the season finale aired this week. Sophie Gilbert: Well, it was one of those shows that became a slow burn, I think. [Theme song from Furious] Rosin: This is staff writer Sophie Gilbert. Gilbert: When it first debuted, there wasn’t that much chatter about it. But then you started to see people watch, and it became this word-of-mouth hit. Rosin: Furious is a dark and sometimes disturbing TV show about a female serial killer, played by Lola Petticrew, who is pursued by a female FBI agent, played by Emmy Rossum. Gilbert: So there’s a lot about it that is quite kind of tropey, old-school procedural. It’s a crime show. The cop and the killer being pursued, they have that kind of, Oh, we’re not so different, you and I, kind of thing going on. But at the same time, it was also like no other procedural I’ve ever seen, in the sense that in so many crime shows, you see women’s bodies used like window dressing almost. And this is a show that really seems to be made about women, not for women necessarily, but it’s interested in women. It’s interested in what happens to women when they go through traumatic experiences, what happens to women when they become angry. There’s so much that is kind of really deep and tied to these mythological elements of transformation and violence. And it just works well on so many levels. Rosin: The show’s mythological elements are in the name. It’s called Furious after the Furies, the Greek goddesses of vengeance. In the show, the Furies are implied to be serial killer Catherine, FBI agent Alice, and Alice’s mentor, Nora—three women who, in different ways, have all failed to find the justice they need. Gilbert: So Nora Washington is the head of the FBI’s sex-crimes unit in the show. She’s played by Quincy Tyler Bernstine in this extraordinary performance. She’s so good. And she has a few speeches where she’s talking to Alice Black, sort of the main character in the show, who’s played by Emmy Rossum, who is trying to become an FBI agent under her wing. And she’s explaining to her the toll that this job takes, of looking into these horrendous sex crimes, these crimes often against underage girls, against children. You take on this responsibility when you do this job of doing this thing that no one else will do, to try and achieve a measure of justice, or certainly a measure of justice that is often impossible, and it changes you. Quincy Tyler Bernstine (as Nora Washington in Furious): Everyone likes it when there’s a sweet little woman lying on the floor, naked and cut up in pieces. I get so fucking angry. Gilbert: Because you have to become, in some ways, a monster to do this day after day. Bernstine: It doesn’t matter, anything you do. The ones who are really to blame don’t get caught. Never. Never. Gilbert: So there are all these sort of elemental themes of Greek tragedy and Greek drama that seem to come through. Bernstine: You think you’re ever gonna catch anyone who matters? Gilbert: So this show starts with a scene of a woman whose name we later find out is Catherine—she’s played by Lola Petticrew—who is keeping a man prisoner in a Brooklyn row house on Halloween. [Sounds from Furious] Gilbert: And Catherine is wearing a mask, and she is eating candy corn, and she is clearly torturing this man. And then eventually, we see her murder him. Lola Petticrew (as Catherine Grace in Furious): I don’t really like listening to you. I don’t like the sounds you’re making. Gilbert: And the show begins in this really stark way of saying, This is who this character is. Like, Be horrified by this; be appalled by her actions. It’s sort of really uncomfortable to watch in lots of ways, really visceral. And then as the show goes on, you understand more about who she is. You understand her history. You understand why she’s doing what she’s doing, her flawed but in some ways very sympathetic logic. And you see her full humanity. And she becomes, yes, a serial killer, but one who does seem to be doing it for reasons that are, if not fully justifiable, you start to sort of empathize with them a little bit more. Rosin: Yeah. And here’s the difficult thing: The parallels to the current world are apparent. This is essentially a Jeffrey Epstein setup. It’s a setup about people who are portrayed as rich. There’s a man at the center of it. There’s a sort of a twisted luring in of teenagers and young women. It really has obvious parallels to the world we are currently living in. And here’s a woman exacting justice because the justice system wouldn’t. Gilbert: Yes. Rosin: So as I describe it, it is sympathetic. You are, in some ways, supposed to root for this person who at the very first scene is gruesome. Gilbert: I don’t know if you’re supposed to root for her, but it becomes impossible not to, in some ways. Rosin: Yeah, yeah. Gilbert: And I think that’s part of the trick. The show is not black and white morally. It reveals things, and it explains them, and it offers context for them. And we, as human beings, watch it, and we have our own context, and we have our own life experiences, and we add. And we’re supposed to make our own judgments, but I don’t think the show is telling us what to sort of presume one way or another. And that, to me, is what makes it so interesting as an experience. But yes, this character Jay Easton is, obviously—he’s certainly in the Jeffrey Epstein mold. He’s a billionaire. He’s revealed to have preyed on hundreds, maybe thousands of young, underage women. And yet, what again is striking about the show is that he’s not really interesting. He’s not a character who the show is sort of interested in delving into, really. The show is much more curious about the impact he’s had on the lives of women and girls, and that, I think, is often what goes underplayed or what is missing in our Epstein discourse as well. So it’s shining a light on a different facet of this very topical issue. [Music] Rosin: As I watched episode after episode, I had a very uncomfortable reaction that I’m guessing other people had, that the creator of the show, Liz Meriwether—who we’ll talk to later—says she intended: I was not, not rooting for the serial killer, this deeply unlikable, twisted, dark, criminal young woman who was effectively hunting down the men who had abused her when she was a teenager. Gilbert: Without being, like, morally endorsing murder, it can be cathartic to see where they go with it and to imagine what happens when there’s no justice possible. What do you do with all that rage? Rosin: Sophie wrote about the show recently for The Atlantic, about how the grief, anger, and rage in Furious reminded her of a different time, nearly a decade ago, when similar feelings of anger generated headlines, spawned think pieces and hashtags, and started the MeToo movement that ultimately fizzled out. Rosin: Yeah. So what does that reflect in the culture then? A sense of frustration, helplessness? What does that mean? Gilbert: For me, the show really resonated when I was thinking about—first of all, it’s been almost a decade since the MeToo moment, which is just wild to think about anyway, all this time. But when you think about what happened at the end of 2017, the revelations about Harvey Weinstein, the revelations about all these men— Reporter (from ABC News): New Yorker magazine reporting new claims of sexual harassment, assault, and rape. One of his accusers going to police, secretly recording her confrontation with Weinstein, but no charges were ever filed. Gilbert: —there was so much in the sense that we were in this moment of societal transformation and women’s anger. There were so many books written about women’s anger. There were TV shows written about women’s anger. It seemed like rage and fury, and righteous fury, was this great theme in our culture that might have a kind of revolutionary force, that it might help upend systems and overturn injustice. Reporter (from CBS Miami): Instead of naming one person, Time magazine named its 2017 Person of the Year the “silence breakers,” the name given to the women who came forward to report sexual harassment and assault, sparking the MeToo movement. Gilbert: And then you look nine years later and you think, Wow, actually, none of that has happened. We’ve, if anything, lost rights. Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been. More and more injustices and horrific crimes against women and girls are revealed. I mean, really, it feels almost daily. We have an overtly misogynist president, I would say. And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb, I think. And so what this show is doing, which really connected with my own sense of just being unable to feel that rage day after day after day, is wondering what happens when it becomes something else, when it takes a different direction, when it realizes that justice is impossible, and so vengeance is the next best thing. Rosin: Hmm. I wanna ask about the broad sweep of things. In your book, Girl on Girl, the thesis is that pop culture taught Millennial women to hate themselves, or maybe just that pop culture of the ’90s and aughts hated women in a certain way. This is a show conceived of by women, written by women, in which a woman and the Furies do get revenge. Does that at least agency, even if it’s a perverse agency, does that represent something different, like controlling the narrative? Gilbert: Yes, the stories that we get now about women, about the complexities of their lives, the conditions that they’re living under, like the truth of their experience, are made by women about women. There’s so much that is so much better than it was even 10 years ago. And I was reading an interview with Liz Meriwether, the creator of Furious, where she said—because she’s the creator of a much-beloved sitcom, one of my favorites, called New Girl—and she was mentioning the notes that she got from Fox in terms of sort of making the character more likable and making it broadly more appealing to men, and how now, making this show, Furious, there was none of that. There’s much more appetite I think, or at least more understanding on the part of people commissioning work like this, that you can be interested in women as a subject and that will make great art that will connect with viewers and be enough of a justification. We don’t need to always be kind of shushing women in a way. Rosin: Yeah. And it’s not just, you can be interested in women. You can be interested—I mean, the task she’s setting out for a viewer here is: You can be interested in a woman who’s, like you said, a monster. From the very first scene, she’s the exact opposite of a beautiful dead victim. She couldn’t be less likable, at least in the very beginning. Gilbert: Yes. And the show really trusts us as audiences to see that and to keep watching, which I think is fascinating all on its own. Like, there’s this idea that we don’t need to be coddled into finding this woman cute and sexy. (Laughs.) Rosin: Yeah. Gilbert: We can see what she is and we can be hooked anyway, because we’re sophisticated enough consumers of media to understand that the payoff might be worth it. [Music] Rosin: After the break, we talk to the Furious showrunner, Liz Meriwether, about why she created a monster you don’t necessarily hate. [Break] [Music] Rosin: Liz Meriwether started as a comedy writer. As Sophie mentioned, her breakout hit was New Girl. Then she wrote The Dropout, a show about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes—also not a classic lovable type. And then Dying for Sex, about a woman who has a terminal-cancer diagnosis—so potentially a perfect victim—but instead, she decides to spend her final months having a lot of sex. We’ve talked a lot on this episode about post-MeToo progress being stalled. But this—this creation, by female writers, of female characters who test the bounds of likability—is also a kind of progress. I talk to Meriwether—who is in the writers’ room working on Season 2 of Furious—about how her ability to write female characters exactly how she wants them has evolved. [Music] Rosin: So the terrible word that’s imposed on female characters forever, which is likable—female politicians, everybody, likability. From the very first scene, you make the decision to make Catherine not likable. Did you get any pushback on that? Like, Put some woman in there who is more pure, or a sort of more recognizable person you can attach yourself to? Meriwether: As somebody who’s been doing this for about 15 years now, and when I first started doing it, got that note all the time, I was surprised that I didn’t get that note. Rosin: Can you actually talk about that? ’Cause you were mostly known as a comedy writer. New Girl was the breakout hit, and when you were writing that, what were the conversations like about how weird or unconventional a main character who’s a woman could be? Meriwether: Yeah. The notes I got were, like—the first pilot I wrote was called Sluts. It was kind of Girls before Girls, in a way. It was three girls in New York who just, like, had a lot of sex and just were deciding to get their lives together and sort of stop having so much sex. And this was for Fox. It was never gonna get on the air. But that was the first pilot that I wrote, and I had conversations with executives that were like, She either is smart, or she likes sex, and that was a binary thing that I had to genuinely have a conversation with somebody about, where I was like, No, you can be smart and also have had a lot of sex. Rosin: So you were in your 20s when you wrote that pilot, when you wrote Sluts. Meriwether: Yeah, I was, like, 25 or something. Yeah. Rosin: And did you already know, I’m trying to push against some kind of tropes or ideas of how female characters should be? Meriwether: Yeah. I mean, I think I’ve always come from a place of, like, I’m gonna make jokes about it or try to come at it from a little bit of a sneakier place. I’ve never been a writer that’s been very I have a big statement I wanna make. Which is, honestly, why this show kinda scared me a little bit, because I was like, I don’t get to hide as much. I don’t get to kind of, like, you know, tap-dance and make jokes and say, like, No, look over here. Look over here. Look over here. But yes, I’ve always been interested in trying to put women on screen that are not what you have seen before. That’s been something that I’ve been interested in for a long time. I just feel like we’ve taken steps forward and steps back over the past 15 years, but there’s definitely more complicated female characters on television now than there was back then. When New Girl first aired, I did a lot of press. It was, like, me and Whitney Cummings had comedies coming out, and [people] were like, We can’t believe there are, like, comedies written by women—more than one comedy written by women. That was like the main thrust of the press. And that would never be a story nowadays. So yes, there, I mean, there is growth. I think that there’s also a lot of moving forward then moving backwards. Rosin: Yeah. For this episode, we also interviewed my Atlantic colleague Sophie Gilbert, who wrote this book Girl on Girl, which is about how pop culture of the late ’90s and aughts hated women or taught Millennial women to hate themselves. And I was thinking about you because you, that’s your era of pop culture. I also saw that you signed on to write the biopic of Britney Spears, who is the ultimate example of how the late ’90s and early aughts chewed some women up. And so I wondered if that was part of what motivates you or what excites you about these kinds of projects. Meriwether: I think so. Yeah. I mean, I do kinda just keep my head down and keep moving forward. Like, I don’t go from a place of like I have an agenda. But yes, those are the characters that really excite me—the women where it’s, like, very hard to put into words how you feel about them. You don’t know if you’re rooting for them or not. I do think it’s a very interesting, fun place to be as a writer, maybe because of all of the notes I got about likability and the desire to sort of get away from that. But I also think it’s not interesting to make somebody completely evil. I think that middle space is really interesting. Rosin: And maybe it just feels more true. Meriwether: Yeah. There’s also a tendency to, say, victimize women in a different way, where it’s like they had no agency in what happened to them or, you know, they are completely products of a broken system, which I feel like is not fair either and a little bit patronizing and boring, honestly. So I think I’m interested in, like, all the nuances of why people do the things they do. [Music] Rosin: Sophie, you know what I was thinking about? The Olivia Rodrigo reprisal of Lilith Fair. Rosin: I don’t know if you saw the documentary about Lilith Fair. Gilbert: I did, yeah. Rosin: So I watched that documentary, and I think I might have cried, honestly, because I thought, Oh, well, that era is dead. Like, We will never, ever have that back again. [Sounds from the Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery trailer] Rosin: A sort of collection of women getting together, talking about their music, entirely made for and run by women, and yet here it is reprised this summer. And I thought, Oh, maybe the sense of agency that’s emerging, it does feel different than what you wrote about [in your book]. It does feel different than the Britney Spears era, the era in which women died by those cultural stories. Now it feels like they’re writing the stories, and so even though they might be grim or they might be inspirational, they are controlling the narrative. Gilbert: That Lilith documentary was so good and I think so sad, for exactly the reasons that you said, which was: It seemed the last moment when this idea of a women-centric society, or at least an alternative society, seemed possible. (Laughs.) And then everything that happened afterwards in the 2000s, and just this real decade of victimizing women for living their lives in public. But yes, again, we have this moment of a mainstream pop star holding a massive music festival for abortion-rights charities and reproductive rights, which you can’t imagine someone like Taylor Swift doing that. Rodrigo: Today I’m so aware of all the women who came before me, who fought for me to enjoy the rights that I enjoy today. Gilbert: All right, it’s not as subversive and as edgy as what riot-grrrl musicians were doing in the ’90s, but it’s political. It’s active. It’s angry about the way that things are, and it’s willing to take a stand to change them. And then it also—I think the thing that I found so fascinating about this festival, Daisy Chain, was that it just demonstrates the power that women have in the music industry. Of all the different cultural industries, music really seems to be one where women are dominant right now—where they sell the most records, where they’re making the most interesting music, where they’re the ones that we are drawn to. They have these huge tours, and they have this huge fandom, and they are front and center in music and powerful in a way that men are not. And that, I think, is interesting right now, in this moment. And the question of why, I don’t know. But if we’re looking for things to be hopeful about, that’s definitely one. Rosin: Right, ’cause in thinking about women’s anger, I got stuck in a kind of limited narrative, which is, Oh, in 2017, women were able to channel the anger in a productive direction. People told their stories. Sort of a dam burst open. There were truths out there, and that was cathartic. And in 2026, we get a serial killer. So then I was trying to think, Well, maybe that’s not that simple. There are places that anger finds an out that are more joyful or productive, and so this is one that I look to. Gilbert: Yeah. Olivia Rodrigo just released a song called “Serena Joy,” which is named, obviously, after the character in The Handmaid’s Tale who has helped subjugate other women. One of the lyrics in it is, “If you can’t throw a punch, you can learn how to spit.” [“Serena Joy,” by Olivia Rodrigo] Gilbert: Just, it’s this idea that numbness is not inevitable. We don’t have to just be complacent forever and ever and ever while our rights are eroded and things are taken away—that in some ways, cultural power is still there, and that there are still women sort of taking a stand for things, and in some ways, storytelling is able to do such interesting work now because we are in a different place than we were in 2017, and we’re much more open to ideas about what’s possible, even if it doesn’t seem like it’s easily achievable. Rosin: Yeah. Well, Sophie, thank you so much for talking this through with me today. Gilbert: Oh, it’s a pleasure. Thank you for having me. [Music] Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes and Jinae West with help from Jacob Smollen. It was edited by Claudine Ebeid. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Fact-checking by Sam Fentress. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

item.title: How the Early Dreams of the Internet Changed
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 4.09
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. During the 1984 Super Bowl, an advertisement launched a technological revolution. If you were alive, you probably know the one. Directed by Ridley Scott, the minute-long spot showed men in gray uniforms, heads shaved, eyes blank, marching in unison toward a lifeless auditorium. A Big Brother figure speaks from a giant screen, droning on about “the first glorious anniversary of the Information Purification Directives.” All the while, a woman in red shorts and a white tank top is running to the auditorium. She looks like she’s just come from an aerobics class, but she has a sledgehammer, and authorities are in pursuit. Entering the room, she hurls the sledgehammer into Big Brother’s face. There’s a flash of light, and a wind blows over the stunned, awakened audience. A different voice—a comforting one—announces, “On January 24th, Apple Computer will introduce Macintosh. And you’ll see why 1984 won’t be like 1984.” Although the ad did not show an actual Macintosh computer, it worked. Apple went on to sell 250,000 of its user-friendly, mouse-driven little machines in that year alone. The ad also asserted what was to be a defining idea of the emerging digital age: that personal computers, far from massive instruments of centralized control, were vessels of individual freedom. The coming of the internet, with its invitation to universally accessible knowledge and the free exchange of ideas, seemed to affirm the promise: Our machines wouldn’t enslave us; they would liberate us. The dystopia depicted in the ad came by way of George Orwell’s imagination, but the fears underlying it had deep American roots. As mass consumer culture expanded in the early 20th century, American artists, intellectuals, and critics worried over the problem of “conformity” and the loss of individualism that came with it. Most didn’t see the dark totalitarianism of 1984; instead, they saw a world of ready-made desires, a soulless existence brought to you by corporations, advertisers, media, and politicians. As The Atlantic’s review of Sinclair Lewis’s Babbitt put it in 1922, “the ‘standardized American’” was becoming “as much a national product as the Ford car”—a person like Babbitt himself, whose entire life and very personality were shaped by forces beyond him. Such criticism formed a fault line that ran from the cultural commentary of the ’20s to the outbursts of Beats, folkies, and academics in the ’50s. The earthquake, of course, would come in the counterculture of the 1960s. No longer would people need to be stuffed into “Little Boxes,” as the folk singer Malvina Reynolds worried early in the decade. The counterculture promised liberation from such confinement. Visiting San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury district for The Atlantic in 1967, the novelist Mark Harris wondered whether he was seeing Babbitt’s descendants finally rebelling against conformity in ways that Babbitt himself could not. The counterculture’s sensibilities migrated into the mainstream, where popular culture and advertising absorbed its language of liberation and transgression, so that admen could pitch 7 Up using hippie iconography or Virginia Slims cigarettes by way of the women’s-liberation movement. Digital culture would prove especially receptive to these countercultural ideals. Northern California, after all, was the center of both the counterculture and the tech industry, and the cross-pollination between the two was considerable, as the historian Fred Turner has shown. By the 1990s, as the internet was becoming a mass medium, some of its first boosters (many of whom had roots in the counterculture) were presenting it as the realization of countercultural ideals. John Perry Barlow, a poet and sometimes Grateful Dead lyricist, wrote his 1996 “Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace” in response to an early effort to regulate the internet. It reads like a Port Huron Statement for digital culture, describing a realm of individual freedom and free-flowing ideas that would break from existing forms of cultural and institutional authority. According to Barlow, a new “civilization of the Mind” was coming. In the dot-com and digital revolutions that followed, many of the people who sold the hardware, coded the software, and built the platforms were seen as iconoclasts themselves. Digital entrepreneurship became a form of transgression, not just in the casual dress and informal culture of the Silicon Valley office but also in what it promised to users. Tech visionaries pledged to create a world that would make possible precisely the kind of self-expression, open exchange, and communal connection that the counterculture had promised. It was no coincidence that by the late 1990s, Apple’s advertising—again with almost no reference to the machines themselves—simply pictured groundbreaking figures such as Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., Bob Dylan, and John Lennon, alongside the slogan “Think Different.” In many ways, those promises were fulfilled. The internet did splinter 20th-century mass culture, and the effects have been every bit as revolutionary as promised. We don’t all watch the same networks anymore; we don’t see the same movies; we don’t get our news from the same places or read the same books (mostly, we just don’t read); we “do our own research.” Even as the conditions of mass culture and conformity that shaped the counterculture and the early dreams of the internet have faded, we continue to live in their shadow. In the fractured age of social media and the unknowable algorithm, our devices give us the feeling of freedom, even as they serve the interests of corporate forces that track our movements, catalog our interests, and profile our wants. The oppressive monoculture has been replaced by countless minicultures, each with their own devoted acolytes; we still inhabit little boxes, partially of our own making. The transgressive ethos, meanwhile, continues to thrive. Subversion is perhaps the dominant language of digital culture, spoken across the political spectrum by podcasters “just asking questions,” wellness gurus swilling at-home health hacks, manosphere kingpins lashing out against wokeness, and lefty influencers denouncing the billionaire class. Everyone, it seems, is hurling a sledgehammer at something.

item.title: The Dead-Internet Theory Is Back
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 4.05
Five years ago, people who hang out in the stranger corners of the web started arguing that the internet was mostly fake. It had been this way since about 2016, they said, when Google introduced its artificial neural network for machine translation. Supposedly, from that point forward, online interactions began to be replaced, until nearly every message and picture had been posted by a bot. Everywhere you looked, websites were “empty and devoid of people,” as one scholar of the theory put it. This wasn’t true, but the core idea was tethered to a real phenomenon. Even way back then, in 2021, social platforms were awash in fake views, fake likes, fake traffic, and fake engagement. Some people figured that automation might one day take over the entire web and then our world. They were mostly being silly, or paranoid. Today they seem like … prophets? “Dead Internet” theory is seeing a revival, this time in mainstream conversation. It’s no longer strange to think that AI might be everywhere, edging out all forms of human interaction: bots talking to bots, all the way down. Every week we seem to take another step in that direction. In June, the Pew Research Center reported that nearly a quarter of American adults now use chatbots every day. Two months later, OpenAI announced an official ChatGPT integration for iMessage. Chatbot-generated text is already widely used for website filler, business emails, and cover letters. Will it soon be commonplace in private messages between friends and family? The ChatGPT-iMessage integration works on your desktop, not your phone. It doesn’t send messages on your behalf until you’ve reviewed and approved its suggestions. A similar plug-in has long been available for Anthropic’s Claude, and many messaging apps already offer AI-suggested replies. To some extent, OpenAI’s new product simply formalizes something that people had been doing on their own, either by pasting text from one window to another, or by improvising personal ChatGPT-linking software. (The Atlantic has a corporate partnership with OpenAI.) “Low-effort communication has always existed,” Michael Pfister, a software developer living in Colorado, told me. He said that he had already vibe coded his own version of the iMessage tool months ago. ChatGPT pings him daily to let him know if he’s missed any important questions in his group chat. He tried having it write a text to his friends, just as an experiment, but they immediately noticed that the message was AI. “They tried to prompt-inject me,” he said: They asked the agent what Michael thought of them, in the hopes of tricking it into sharing his private thoughts. He told me that he mostly uses the tool for work and that he isn’t interested in having AI communicate with his friends on his behalf in the future. “I think relationships are experiential,” he said. Max Weinbach, an analyst at a market-research firm in Connecticut, told me he uses ChatGPT to text with his bosses about work. “It just makes life easy,” he said. It’s hardly different from using Google’s suggested email responses, which have been available for nearly a decade. Weinbach had no ethical qualms about switching to LLM-assisted communication, although he recognizes that it can be taken as a sign of disrespect. “It’s not accepted or polite,” he said. “It’s just kind of a rude thing to do.” These two are on the bleeding edge, yet exhibiting more restraint than some others. All over Reddit, my favorite repository for human drama, people are worrying about human drama that has a nonhuman interloper. New posts appear each day requesting help in figuring out whether something might have been created with AI: Is this apartment listing real? What about this dating-app profile? What about this video of a cute animal doing something amazing? (A bobcat flagging down a biker to help her rescue her kitten from the bottom of a random hole?) Many of the requests have a moralistic tone, and the poster comes to the crowd solemnly, with hesitation, because they know the truth may be painful. The most fraught discussions concern AI-generated personal messages. Guys on dating apps are using the technology. Sometimes long-term partners, friends, siblings, or parents do it too. “Is this text apology written by ChatGPT?” someone will ask. Or “Did my mother use ChatGPT to write me a text of support on the morning of my divorce?” The implication is betrayal. I spoke with Melissa Crowder, a 47-year-old from Alberta, Canada, who shared her own experience with AI texting in a July post on Reddit. She’d spent all day having a “nice conversation” with a match from the dating app Feeld, then finally noticed that their repartee was off when he copy-pasted her own message back to her by mistake. At that point she realized all of his previous messages had been structurally similar—usually two paragraphs of text followed by a question on a single line. And he’d been using the word dangerously way too much. When she asked if he was using ChatGPT, he replied, “Busted” with a bunch of emoji, which also struck her as something ChatGPT might do. “I’m like, this is still ChatGPT.” Then he unmatched her. Crowder would not have been that mad if the guy had just fessed up and said something normal in his own voice. She sometimes uses AI tools to help her express herself too. She said she has a tendency to ramble on and overexplain her feelings, so she’ll use a site called Goblin Tools to self-edit. She might make a message to her ex-husband “Less emotional” (one of the choices in a drop-down menu) and get straight to the point. She also has a friend who sends AI-written texts from time to time. “Where I would draw my line is where you take the person out of the conversation,” she said. “If I’m vibing with a chatbot and then I meet the person in real life, what is that conversation going to look like?” For a recent paper, a group of researchers from the University of Washington and Arizona State University studied two popular Reddit forums—r/RealOrAI and r/isthisAI—to figure out how people go about determining which material is AI-generated and which is not. The most common mode of analysis evaluates the fundamental plausibility of an image or a video. (“Babies do not nearly have that much coordination to both be standing up, talking so well and holding up that large cat.”) A smaller number of comments in the study addressed some alleged telltale signs of AI-style texting, including the prevalence of “overly ornate but meaningless phrases.” Other people have noted LLMs’ overreliance on certain words (delve is an oft-noted one), sentence structures (negative parallelisms), and punctuation (em dashes). The paper ends in an ominous tone. “Our findings suggest that people are developing mental models of what AI-generated content looks like, built on personal experiences and beliefs developed over time,” the authors wrote, before arguing that these mental models were unlikely to be accurate for long. The LLMs will evolve and stop doing the things that now make their output so easy to spot. In fact, the tricks enumerated in the paper are already getting old, one of the paper’s authors, Tina Yeung, told me. “I definitely think this is a snapshot in time,” she said. The mere fact of people’s concern about AI, and their anxiety over its incursion into day-to-day life, may be a snapshot too. Perhaps the stigma that now exists around using ChatGPT to text a friend or message on a dating app will fade in the years ahead. Maybe one day it will disappear altogether, and even our phones will end up empty and devoid of people. Or else I guess it’s possible—just possible—that the Dead Internet theory is as silly as it ever was.

item.title: The Dark Side of Mindfulness
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 3.82
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. In 2004, Willoughby Britton, then a doctoral candidate in clinical psychology at the University of Arizona, began recruiting participants for a study that, she felt sure, would show meditation improves sleep. Britton, a meditation teacher, was so devoted to the practice that she saw herself as a “double agent,” someone who uses science to promote meditation. Although she had grown up in a nonpracticing Episcopalian home, she’d become deeply invested in Buddhist teachings. She read meditation books in her spare time and at one point considered becoming a Buddhist nun. She was confident that meditation improved most things, including sleep; it had already improved much about her own life. For her study, Britton split 26 participants into two groups: one that would go through an eight-week-long meditation class, and one that would serve as a control group. She brought them all into a lab to sleep overnight while sensors measured their brain waves, muscle activity, and eye movements. But when she reviewed the results, she was dismayed to find they were the opposite of what she had predicted. The participants in the meditation group slept more fitfully, with more frequent awakenings, than those who didn’t meditate. They spent more time in “Stage 1,” the lightest sleep phase, from which people are easily roused. “Graph after graph after graph, no matter how you looked at it—number of awakenings, number of micro arousals, number of Stage 1 minutes,” Britton told me, the amount of meditation that the subjects practiced was directly correlated with worse sleep quality. Britton wasn’t sure what had happened. Had she done something wrong? Designed the study poorly? Was the result a fluke, a random finding that didn’t mean much? Or perhaps meditators just need less sleep. At the time, promoting meditation was more important to her than scientific ethics, and she worried that publishing the results would mean “harming the dharma”—criticizing the teachings of the Buddha. So she didn’t. On a meditation retreat not long after this, she was chatting about her study with a meditation teacher when the teacher said, “I don’t know why all you psychologists try to make meditation into a relaxation technique. Everyone knows if you meditate enough, you stop sleeping.” On some level, Britton must have known this. At that point, she had spent years both meditating and studying the brain. Because most kinds of meditation aim to enhance concentration, the practice can act like a stimulant. And just as chemical stimulants such as caffeine and Adderall can interfere with sleep, so, too, can excessive meditation. What else, she wondered, did meditation teachers know that they weren’t telling people? Gradually, starting with that sleep study, the tiers of thought propping up Britton’s worldview—that Buddhism is a cure-all, and that meditation was always beneficial, and could never cause harm—would collapse. Over time, she would find that meditation, a multibillion-dollar industry that is promoted as a treatment for anxiety, chronic pain, alcohol abuse, addiction, and many other ailments, can sometimes, for some people, cause severe and lasting side effects: depression, anxiety, even acute psychosis. Losing the belief system that had been foundational to her life would lead her to produce a trailblazing body of research about the adverse effects of meditation, and then to found a clinical practice geared toward helping the people—a lot of them, as it turns out—who believe that meditation has harmed them. Britton has straight blond hair, blue eyes, and a muted affect. When you say something to her, she pauses, as if considering whether or not to smile. A colleague once suggested to her that she might be autistic. “And I’m like, ‘Okay,’” she told me one day recently. She grew up on a farm in Massachusetts with parents who believed that a person should find a problem that isn’t being solved and embrace it as their niche. Her father’s niche was fermenting waste from local businesses and selling it as compost. Britton was, by her own description, a weird kid who spent a lot of time by herself. She was always asking strange questions like “What is looking out of my eyes?” One day during the summer break after her junior year at Colgate University, where she was majoring in neuroscience, Britton went over to the house of her best friend, Sarah, a champion athlete at Dartmouth, and discovered her lying lifeless on the bed, a hunting rifle on the floor and a splatter of blood on the wall. Overwhelmed by the pressure of competitive sports, Sarah had taken her own life. After Sarah’s death, Britton developed symptoms of PTSD. She grew afraid of crossing the street and of driving. She didn’t like opening doors, because she feared she might find a dead body behind them. At one point, while killing rats at her bench in the National Institutes of Health lab where she worked between college and graduate school, she watched the blood drain from their eyes and wondered aloud to a colleague, “Where does it go?” “In the freezer,” the colleague responded. But Britton wasn’t asking about the rat’s body, but its life force. Where did that go? She was reluctant to take medication, so her father sent her the book A Path With Heart, by the famous meditation teacher Jack Kornfield. She appreciated Kornfield’s explanation for why humans are so prone to rumination—“over and over we feel the familiar tug of thoughts and reactions that take us away from the present moment,” he writes—and that he offered a way out via meditation. She began meditating for half an hour to an hour each day. In graduate school, Britton initially focused her research on the neuroscience of near-death experiences, but for her dissertation she pivoted to studying meditation, which had been so steadying for her personally. Meditation was, even then, having a moment. In 2005, the filmmaker David Lynch established a foundation that aimed to promote Transcendental Meditation in colleges and schools. Soon, tech CEOs were flocking to mindfulness summits to learn about “wisdom in the workplace” or “conscious leadership,” and a mindfulness class for Google employees regularly had a long waiting list. High-powered celebs including Oprah and Arianna Huffington credited meditation for centering them amid their empire building. LeBron James partnered with Calm, a multibillion-dollar meditation-and-sleep app. Today, according to one study, about half of all Americans have tried meditation, and about a fifth meditate regularly. Meditation’s popularity is well-founded. Although the practice has long been supported by the more woo-woo corners of the wellness industry, as well as by Eastern philosophy, an accumulating body of scientific research has suggested that it has all kinds of measurable benefits. Major studies show that meditation can alleviate anxiety and depression—at least about as well as the antidepressant Lexapro can, but without the cost and with fewer side effects. Even short periods of meditation have shown notable effects on the brain: Several studies have found that eight weeks of meditation training can reduce reactivity in the amygdala, the emotion center of the brain, and another showed that meditation could help activate brain regions involved in attention, memory, and perspective-taking in people with social-anxiety disorder. Other reputable studies have linked meditation to positive mood; improved immune function; reduced chronic inflammation; less back pain; lower blood pressure; enhanced self-awareness; better attention spans; greater compassion; and even reduced feelings of loneliness in older adults. Beyond the scientific evidence, Britton believes that meditation became popular because it’s a health hack that people can do independently, without relying on expensive medical care. The practice suggests that “underneath all of your thinking is some beautiful, basic state” just waiting to be discovered, she said. It probably helps, she added, that meditation is “this ancient thing from Asia and therefore seems more legit or real or something.” In graduate school, Britton became a serious meditator in the Western insight tradition, which includes sitting and focusing on an “anchor,” such as one’s breath, sometimes for hours at a time. Britton describes it as an austere practice intended to “train the mind.” She molded her life around ancient Buddhist principles. When colleagues remarked on her plain appearance, she said, “Why would I adorn myself?” Soon, Britton immersed herself in Tibetan studies. Instead of reading novels at night, she’d read dharma books. Her belief at this time, she said, was that “getting enlightened is the most helpful thing you could do for the world.” She considered dropping out of academia to move to a monastery in Asia, which would have meant renouncing her former life, taking a vow of celibacy, and living under a new name. But she stayed in the United States and continued her academic work, while also training to teach mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR), a secular meditation program developed in the ’70s by a molecular biologist named Jon Kabat-Zinn, and a related course called mindfulness-based cognitive therapy. These classes promise to help everyday people with their stress, low moods, and chronic pain; alongside daily meditation practice, they typically include some non-Buddhist teachings from psychology and literature. Britton moved to Rhode Island to begin her clinical residency at Brown University’s Warren Alpert Medical School. She didn’t know anyone, and, working 12-hour days, she felt intimidated by the cutthroat Ivy League academic life. To fill the time she had to herself, she started meditating for three hours a day. One night, after meditating on her balcony for an hour, she went back inside and noticed that her house felt like someone else’s home. A picture of her with two friends looked like a picture of three people she happened to know. Britton decided to take a walk, and as she strolled the streets of Providence, she felt like a bird sitting on her own shoulder, watching herself. She walked into a creperie where she noticed two people arguing. When they both turned and glared at her, she thought, Oh my God, I forgot that I am a person. What Britton was experiencing is called dissociation, a state that can occasionally be evolutionarily useful—it can help people push through a task when faced with overwhelming terrors. But according to Britton and other researchers, it can happen to extreme meditators too. Britton told me that extensive meditation can prompt the prefrontal cortex to essentially shut off the brain’s emotional centers, causing feelings to seem blunted. And without the typical emotions that we project onto objects, familiar things—our hands, our homes—can start to look foreign. Heleen Slagter, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam who studies meditation, says that part of the way the brain gives rise to our sense of self is by predicting how we will interact with the world in the future. If you spend enough time zeroing in on the present moment, as one aims to do during meditation, Slagter says, your sense of the future can start to recede—and with it your sense of self. This can produce dissociation. Britton began dissociating a few times a week. She had trouble driving because she couldn’t sense where her body began and ended. She’d watch a sappy commercial and suddenly notice her face was wet, not realizing she had shed tears. She felt porous, like other people’s states of mind were her own, a fact that became especially disturbing when she was treating suicidal patients. The dissociation continued for six or seven years, sometimes happening during meditation, but other times at random. When she told meditation teachers about the dissociation, she said they told her she had entered a new stage of enlightenment—that she was “riding the ox backward.” She had “seen the truth of no-self,” they said, and this was a good thing. They told her to keep meditating, which made the dissociation worse. Somehow, Britton got through her postdoc, but she wasn’t entirely functional. She didn’t date anyone for a decade. Even before she started dissociating, another layer of Britton’s worldview began to crumble after she moved to Rhode Island and was working at an inpatient psychiatric hospital as part of her residency. One day, someone came in from a meditation-retreat center in a state of florid psychosis. Three months later, another psychotic meditator came in, from the same retreat center. That’s weird, Britton thought. Do they know each other? They did not. It’s well known that psychedelics such as LSD can spark psychotic breaks, but meditation can produce altered states of consciousness almost as powerful as those induced by psychedelics. The brain likes and expects a certain amount of input; go long enough without doing anything and the neurons might start to fire spontaneously, producing, say, flashes of light or made-up memories. Inuit people in the Arctic Circle have been known to experience a type of hysteria known as piblokto, which might be brought on by the sensory deprivation of long winters. No one seems to know why, exactly, psychedelics and meditation can both occasionally prompt psychosis, but it might have to do with the fact that both can have the effect of “rewiring your brain,” which can be a positive thing but can also mean your brain just doesn’t work the way it used to. It might become more easily influenced, for example, or impart grave significance on unimportant events. At this point in her research, Britton’s studies were still mostly focused on the benefits of meditation, such as on how it can be helpful for depressed people and substance-abusing teens. But now, when she spoke about her studies at conferences, she’d sometimes briefly mention some of the potential adverse effects of meditation. Afterward, people would corner her in the halls or in the bathroom and tell her they’d had negative experiences with meditation—everything from increased depression to psychotic breaks.
